News.title: Russia names glam suspected assassin ‘who blew up treacherous Ukrainian sub commander after his defection to Putin’
News.content:
RUSSIA has named the glamorous suspected assassin accused of blowing up a former Ukrainian submarine commander who defected to Vladimir Putin’s regime.

Margarita Reutt, 32, allegedly acted as a covert Ukrainian intelligence operative before planting a bomb inside a rubbish bin and remotely detonating it in Sevastopol.



The blast is said to have killed Robert Shageev, 49, a former Ukrainian submarine commander who had defected to Russia and was serving as a Russian Ministry of Defence officer.

Reutt allegedly confessed to carrying out the deadly bombing after being detained by Russia’s FSB.



The explosive device reportedly erupted at around 10am local time, ripping into the officer and leaving him severe injuries, according the the FSB.

The security service said: “As a result of the explosion, the man sustained injuries incompatible with life.



“It was established that the woman, born in 1994, carried out the bombing on the instructions of the Ukrainian special services.”

Mikhail Razvozhaev, Vladimir Putin’s governor of Sevastopol, claimed the FSB was “hot on the heels of the incident” before Reutt was detained.

He said she was suspected of carrying out a “cynical crime” against a Russian officer.

Razvozhaev added: “This is a cynical crime against an officer.



“The perpetrator – born in 1994 – is already giving evidence.

“The investigation has established that she was acting on the orders of the Ukrainian special services and shows no remorse for her actions.”

Reutt was reportedly spotted acting suspiciously in a residential district before ordinary Russians helped authorities track her down.

When interrogators allegedly asked whether she regretted the blast, she reportedly answered: “no”.

The 32-year-old was born in Yaroslavl and previously ran a travel agency which collapsed before she took a job as a biologist.



Her reported final employment was at a laboratory producing floral-infused vaginal suppositories.

She has also reportedly appeared on escort websites.

Reutt lived in the Russian resort of Sochi and allegedly told interrogators she had been “paid for the explosion in cryptocurrency”.



The extraordinary claims come after Reutt was reportedly fined in 2025 for “discrediting the Russian Armed Forces”.

Mash reported she had previously caused outrage aboard a Samara-Adler train when she allegedly shouted: “Serves you right, Russians!”, after news of a drone attack on a railway station.

She also reportedly said she was “ashamed to be Russian”.

Reutt is said to have travelled extensively around Russia and abroad, particularly to Egypt and Turkey.

After the alleged bombing, she reportedly planned to vanish overseas and had already bought a ticket from Sochi.



But her alleged escape plan was foiled when she was detained by Russian authorities and taken in for questioning.

The explosive claims come amid a growing string of alleged Ukrainian covert operations targeting senior Russian military figures deep behind the front line.

In December last year, a concealed car bomb tore through a quiet Moscow district and killed Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov, one of Vladimir Putin’s senior generals.

Sarvarov, who was responsible for training Russia’s armed forces, was killed shortly before 7am when the hidden explosive detonated beneath his vehicle in the Yasenevo district.

It was the third killing of a senior Russian military leader in 2025.



And the latest alleged hit follows another deadly blast at an elite Moscow restaurant packed with Kremlin-linked military figures.

A secret burial was reportedly held for Lt Gen Igor Yerusalimov, 53, at the high-security Troyekurovskoye Cemetery after he was killed in the restaurant bombing.

Yerusalimov was reportedly among five people killed when a homemade device detonated during a lavish birthday gathering for Colonel-General Alexander Chayko.



High-ranking officers, politicians and senior bureaucrats had gathered inside the exclusive Balzi Rossi overlooking Moscow’s Kudrinskaya Square when the bomb exploded.

The device was reportedly carried into the restaurant as a “birthday gift” by a female courier.

The woman carrying it was stopped by a security operative before the package detonated, killing her, the security officer and three others.

A separate report identified one of the dead as Major-General Valeri Plokhotnyuk, a senior Russian officer who was reportedly killed in the same blast on August 1.

Despite alleged attempts by Russian authorities to suppress news of his death, Plokhotnyuk was reportedly buried covertly at Troyekurovskoye Cemetery, in an area reserved for elite military and security officials.



The bomb was reportedly believed to have been intended for Chayko, who escaped the blast unharmed.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Plokhotnyuk was said to be the godfather of Chayko’s daughter Maria, 25, who was seriously wounded in the explosion.

Together, the alleged attacks paint a chilling picture of a shadow war playing out far beyond Ukraine’s front lines, with senior Russian military figures increasingly vulnerable to devastating strikes in their own territory.

News.title: Horror footage shows passengers gasp for breath after ‘aircon failure’ turns plane into furnace during SEVEN HOUR delay
News.content:
OVER 100 passengers on board a plane in New Delhi were left gasping for breath after the air-con failed.

The SpiceJet flight to Pune, India, was readying to leave the Indira Gandhi International Airport when the temperature inside the cabin soared.



Footage from inside the “hot and humid” cabin shows people yelling for help and frantically fanning themselves.

Traveller Leshpal Javalge told local media: “We were drenched in sweat… [there was] no AC or ventilation.



“There were pregnant women, children and elderly passengers onboard. Everyone was scared for their lives. Children began to cry.

“A pregnant woman started feeling breathless and was about to faint. We raised the alarm that she would die if she was not attended to immediately.”



He said the flight was scheduled to depart from New Delhi at 9.55pm on Tuesday but was delayed until 10.30pm.

As passengers entered the aircraft, they noticed the air-con was not working – but assumed it would take some time to start.

Half an hour passed and the cabin turned “extremely hot.”

Javalge added: “The aircraft was completely full and with the doors closed, the heat and humidity became unbearable.”



Passengers grabbed newspapers, magazines and safety cards from their seat pockets to fan themselves and others.

One person could be heard shouting in Hindi: “Tell them to open the gate! Otherwise I’ll break it down.”

Tensions skyrocketed when a few even attempted to open the jet’s main door themselves.



Eventually, their demands were met and they were allowed to deboard, as reported by NeedToKnow.

Another flight was arranged, which departed at around 5.30am the day after – more than seven hours after it was initially scheduled.

A SpiceJet spokesperson said: “On August 11, 2026, SpiceJet flight SG 105, scheduled to operate from Delhi to Pune, encountered a last-minute technical issue.

“An alternate aircraft was arranged, and the flight subsequently operated to Pune.

“SpiceJet deeply regrets the inconvenience caused to the passengers.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

This comes just weeks after another incident, this time on board an Emirates flight from Dubai, UAE, to Shanghai, China, during which 373 passengers were left trapped on the tarmac without air conditioning for 10 hours.

News.title: Passenger train derails near UK station as emergency services flood track and line closed
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TRAIN HORROR Passenger train derails near UK station as emergency services flood track and line closed

A PASSENGER train has derailed near a busy UK station – as emergency services flood the track.

Southern Railway confirmed services would be cancelled until 10pm following the horror near Lewes, East Sussex, this afternoon.



Cops, paramedics and fire crews have been scrambled to the crash after the train derailed at around 3.54pm.

People have been urged to avoid the area as teams swarm the track.



No trains are now able to run through the area and those already travelling have been warned to expect hour-long delays.

British Transport Police said: “Officers are currently on scene close to Lewes railway station following reports of a derailed train at 3.54pm today.



“We’re responding alongside paramedics and the fire service and will provide more information as soon as we can.”

Officers from Sussex Police are also in attendance, the force confirmed.



East Sussex Fire and Rescue said an update on the derailment would be issued at 5pm.

The service said: “We can confirm we were called at 3.55pm to reports that a train had derailed just outside Lewes.

“We are working with other emergency services at the scene.

“Further updates will be given around 5pm.”

Issuing a statement, Southern Railway said: “A train has derailed in the Lewes area. This has closed all lines running through this station.



“As a result of this, trains are currently unable to run through the area to allow the emergency services to attend the incident.

“Major disruption is expected until 22:00.”

News.title: Horror moment Turkey tourist boat erupts in flames as holidaymakers leap into water & 115 are evacuated including kids
News.content:
THIS is the horrific moment a tourist boat erupted into flames in Turkey as holidaymakers leapt overboard and 115 passengers were evacuated.

Shocking footage showed an inferno rip through the pleasure boat and send columns of black, acrid smoke shooting into the sky.



Terrified passengers and crew, including children, were forced to jump into the sea wearing life jackets to escape the raging blaze.

Two people affected by the smoke were rushed to hospital while several children among the 115 evacuated were taken for precautionary medical checks.



The stricken boat was rendered unusable and towed to shore by the coastguard.

While the cause of the fire is not yet clear, it reportedly broke out in the boat’s kitchen around 11am.



Flames quickly ripped through the vessel, sparking a mass evacuation.

Coastguard and marine police squads raced to the scene, while other boats in the area assisted in rescue operations.

The nationalities of those on board were not immediately clear.

However, boat tours along Turkey‘s famed Aegean and Mediterranean coastline are popular with tourists and locals alike.

Authorities have launched an investigation into the cause of the fire.

It comes just weeks after an “overpacked” tourist boat exploded, killing one Brit on board.



Tourists crammed onto the vessel in the Dominican Republic claimed it reeked of petrol and “didn’t feel safe” before the fatal blast.

Abbie Lainton, 16, from Swindon, died after the “terrible accident” while on a family holiday.

Her two siblings were also injured in the incident and remain in hospital.

Abbie died after she was badly burnt when the boat carrying around 35 people suddenly burst into flames off the coast of the Caribbean island.

She was rushed to intensive care on July 27 but died three days later.



Authorities said 24 people were injured with 11 taken to hospital for treatment for burns.

Just last month, a terrifying fire erupted on a £1.7million yacht, forcing three people, including a child, to flee.

Shocking footage showed the luxury vessel engulfed in flames, sending black smoke billowing into the sky, near Sardinia, Italy.

The trio were forced to abandon the floating inferno, reportedly jumping into the sea before the fire consumed the boat.

They were rescued by a nearby vessel and were later transferred to an Italian Coast Guard vessel and taken safely ashore.

News.title: Luigi Mangione expected to plead guilty to federal charges in assassination of CEO Brian Thompson, report says
News.content:
LUIGI Mangione is expected to plead guilty in federal court on Friday in connection with the fatal shooting of UnitedHealthCare CEO Brian Thompson.

The bombshell update comes as Mangione, the 28-year-old Ivy League graduate, was weeks away from going on trial in a separate case in state court on September 8.



Mangione appeared in Manhattan Criminal Court on Tuesday for his final pretrial hearing before jury selection was scheduled to begin.

However, hours after the court was adjourned, an impromptu hearing in federal court was scheduled for Friday morning between Mangione, his defense team, and federal prosecutors.





Now, Mangione, who is facing two federal counts of stalking resulting in death and firearms offenses, is reportedly set to agree to a plea deal, according to The New York Times.

The terms of the plea deal, including what charges Mangione will plead guilty to, remain unclear.

If a federal judge approves the plea deal it could derail Mangione’s impending state trial.

Mangione is facing multiple state charges, including second-degree murder, weapons possession, and possession of a forged instrument.



He is facing up to 25 years to life in prison if the trial moves ahead and he is convicted.

Mangione’s federal trial is scheduled to begin in January 2027.

He pleaded not guilty in both cases.

The Manhattan District Attorney’s Office said it was prepared to lobby the federal judge presiding over Mangione’s case for a stiff sentence should the defendant’s plea deal be approved.

“If a proposed federal guilty plea would operate to defeat a just outcome in the state prosecution, the People could advise the federal district court if that consequence, and the court should consider that fact in deciding whether to accept the plea, as well as any opposition by the victim’s family to such a resolution,” the DA’s office told ABC News.



Since his dramatic extradition to New York in December 2024, Mangione’s lead defense attorney, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, has sought to dismiss the state’s murder indictment on the grounds of double jeopardy.

Double jeopardy prohibits a defendant from being tried for the same crime twice; however, the Manhattan district attorney’s office could argue the state charges against Mangione are different from those in the federal indictment.

Mangione was arrested at a McDonald’s in Altoona, Pennsylvania, on December 9, 2024, after a cashier at the fast food restaurant called police to report that he looked like the shooter from New York.

The shooting of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson sparked a five-day manhunt after the executive was shot in cold blood by a masked, hooded individual outside the Hilton Hotel in Midtown Manhattan on December 4, 2024.

Surveillance footage captured the moment the shooter brazenly sneaks up behind Thompson, 50, and fired several shots from a ghost gun, killing the healthcare executive.



The shooter, suspected to be Mangione, then walks away and is later captured on a surveillance camera jumping on a Citi Bike e-bike and pedals uptown before zooming into Central Park and later exiting around 77th Street.

Video later revealed the gunman walked to 86th Street and Columbus Avenue, where he took a taxi to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Midtown, leaving the New York City area.

News.title: Woman & lover jailed for killing two men in honeytrap plot after spiking drinks with date-rape drug to steal cash
News.content:
LOCKED UP Woman & lover jailed for killing two men in honeytrap plot after spiking drinks with date-rape drug to steal cash

A WOMAN and her lover have been jailed for killing two men in a honeytrap plot after spiking their drinks with a date-rape drug.

Adina Mihai, 31, posed as an escort to take money from from her victims before tricking her way into their homes.



She would secretly lace their drinks with GBL to render them unconscious so she and partner Madalin Dumitru, 30, could steal from the men.

Gary Mouat, 37, and big game hunter Malcolm King, 80, both died as part of the honeypot plot.



Two other men, who can’t be named, were also poisoned by the pair, who are originally from Romania, but survived.

Mihai and Dumitru have now been jailed for 17 years each after they pleaded guilty to manslaughter and two counts of manslaughter and two counts of administering poison with intent to injure.



In a victim impact statement, Gary’s nine-year-old son asked the couple: “Why did you have to kill my dad, you could have just taken the money, he was really kind, he would have given it to you.

“You have ruined my life and all the plans we had to do things together. My family is destroyed now.

“I will never get over my dad being killed, I will never forget him and I will miss him for the rest of my life. I hope I make him proud.”

Oxford Crown Court heard the men hired Mihai expecting sexual services for around £170 an hour through a Vivastreet website.



Dumitru would drive her to an address and wait outside as she drugged her victims.

Mihai then stole watches, jewellery, aftershave and cash – although the value of the pilfered goods is not known.

Gary was discovered dead at his home in Banbury, Oxfordshire, on July 13 last year.



Once officers found he had been poisoned, Thames Valley Police issued a national bulletin to all other forces to share intelligence on other unexplained deaths.

Malcolm’s death on August 21, 2024, had initially been put down to a pre-existing health condition.

But following the alert, Gloucestershire Police re-examined his death and found he died after drinking wine laced with GBL.



Police believe Mihai and Dumitru stole his Rolex before fleeing his £4million Cotswolds home – leaving him to die alone.

He was found the following morning lying on the floor of the lounge by family friends, who were concerned he had not been in contact with anyone since the previous day.

An open bottle of wine was found nearby with two wine glasses.

Julian Evans KC, prosecuting, said: “In summary, Adina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru drugged their victims via the administration of GBL, a potent drug, concealed in alcohol,” he said.

“They did so with a specific purpose in mind: to render their victims unconscious inside their homes in order to steal property from them.



“To carry out this plan, the defendants offered sexual services from a woman to each victim for money.

“After contact was made through a website, and arrangements made by phone, Mihai and Dumitru drove to the home address of each victim.

“While Dumitru waited nearby, Mihai would enter the victim’s home. There, she would persuade the victim to drink alcohol laced with GBL to render them unconscious.

“Once the victim was unconscious, Mihai would look for property to steal. Then she would rejoin Dumitru, leaving the victim alone and unconscious.”

The court heard the third victim was poisoned after contacting Mihai on the escort site just hours after she killed Gary.



She arrived at his home with Dumitru in the early hours of the morning with a bottle of wine bought at a petrol station.

The man handed over £450 and slipped unconscious after drinking some of the alcohol – before waking up to find his watch missing.

A week later, the fourth victim, contacted Mihai and she arranged to meet for £360.

He drank vodka laced with GBL and had jewellery, aftershave and some documents stolen.

Officers are now keeping an open mind about the possibility of other victims but no other deaths or poisonings have been linked to the couple.



Detective Inspector Adam Stacey, of Gloucestershire’s major crime investigation team, urged anyone to come forward if they believe they are victims due to the large gap in offending.

“We worked with the National Crime Agency and other forces in efforts to identify whether there were other victims that may have died as a result of their crimes,” he said.

“There may well be other victims who have survived such druggings, or other targeting from them, but there have been no other homicide victims that we’ve been able to identify.

“We did identify some living victims during the course of our investigation, some of which featured in our case, others didn’t feature, so we know there are other victims out there.

“We do fully understand the sensitivities around why a victim might not want to come forward to us.



“The personal circumstances and the nature of what goes on is very obvious, but we are here to support those individuals, and I would encourage those victims to come forward.”

News.title: Britain defends seizing Putin’s shadow fleet tankers fuelling Ukraine war after tyrant threatened to ‘respond in kind’
News.content:
BRITAIN has defended its seizure of a Russian shadow fleet tanker after Vladimir Putin ominously threatened to “respond in kind”.

The beleaguered tyrant lashed out after one of his shadowy network of sanctioned vessels was captured in the English Channel.



Russia has been operating a shadow fleet of oil tankers to evade international sanctions, fuel its war-ravaged economy and fund its illegal war in Ukraine.

Elite Royal Marines Commandos boarded one such ship – The Smyrtos – and captured its 25 crew in a first-of- its-kind operation in June.



Dramatic footage of its seizure released by the MoD showed how marines fast-roped from helicopters during the six-hour operation.

The Smyrtos has since been anchored off Weymouth and its captain, Ajay Pant, has been charged with breaching Russian sanctions.

He has also been accused of directly or indirectly supplying or delivering prohibited Russian oil.

Putin blasted the seizure while overseeing Russian navy drills in the Pacific, branding the operation as “nothing other than piracy and banditry”.

The dictator menacingly warned that if Western countries seize more tankers, then Russian “will have to respond in kind”.

He added: “And not necessarily in the waters where raids on our ships and vessels are planned, but wherever we deem it necessary and appropriate, anywhere.”



His fleet commander Admiral Viktor Liina said he had identified 26 British commercial vessels since April in Russia’s exclusive economic zone.

Liina declared: “We have the capabilities to inspect and detain vessels from unfriendly states and their shadow fleet.

“We are ready to begin tackling these tasks.”



In response to Putin’s comments, the UK defended its seizure of the Smyrtos as being “in full accordance with international law“.

A government spokesperson said: “The UK is disrupting and deterring shadow fleet vessels and their harmful maritime activity which is fuelling Russia’s war with Ukraine.”

They added that, unlike Russia’s shadow fleet, Britain’s “armed forces and commercial vessels operate firmly in line with international maritime law”.

The UK’s Ministry of Defence has said that Russia operates more than 700 shadow tankers smuggling 75 per cent of its sanctioned oil.

To evade detection, they turn off tracking systems, falsify location data, and conduct ship-to-ship transfers at sea to disguise the oil’s origin.



These vessels – often older and poorly maintained – are accused of using complex ownership structures and flying under other nations’ flags to avoid detection.

The oil ferried is a “critical lifeline for the Kremlin” in “sustaining Russia’s illegal war” in Ukraine, the MoD said.

The Smyrtos continues to be detained and monitored by British authorities in Weymouth, while 22 of its 25 crew have been repatriated.



A Sun investigation revealed at least 28 ‘banned’ boats have been caught on radar transiting the channel since June 19.

It has sparked calls for more action from new PM Andy Burnham in the Channel to hit Russia‘s global oil trade empire where it hurts.

But Putin said he would be “forced to respond in kind,” if Russian ships continued to be targeted.

Retaliation would occur wherever the dictator “considers necessary and appropriate”, including “within the Pacific Fleet’s area of responsibility”.

Putin warned: “I would ask you to pay attention to this.



“The Defence Ministry has been given such an instruction, and I know that it has also been passed on to the Pacific Fleet command.”

Putin’s security council number two Dmitry Medvedev rammed home the Russian threat.

“The overwhelming majority of Western European vessels also sail under flags of convenience,” he said.

“And what does that mean?

“It means that, following a symmetrical approach, which is only fair, Russia has the right to attack any merchant vessel belonging to hostile countries, whether in our waters or in neutral waters, if there are sufficient grounds to suspect that it is carrying cargo in the interests of the enemy.



“In other words, any cargo at all.”

News.title: Karoline Leavitt’s best bits as WH press sec – from sparring with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, ‘your mom’ joke & ‘stupid’ jibe
News.content:
KAROLINE Leavitt has delivered plenty of fiery one-liners from the White House podium – and she is leaving the job on a high.

The 28-year-old press secretary is stepping down at the end of the month after 18 months as one of President Donald Trump’s most recognizable and trusted aides.



Trump announced her departure Wednesday, saying Leavitt wanted to spend more time with her family.

The president said it was “a decision I totally understand and respect!” and revealed she will remain in his orbit as “one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party.”



Leavitt, the youngest White House press secretary in history, described the job as “the honor and adventure of a lifetime.”

She added: “Most of all, I am thankful to the President for entrusting me with the distinct privilege of speaking on his behalf at the White House podium.

“I have relished holding the liberal media accountable and ensuring the American people hear the truth about President Trump’s successes.”

Her departure brings the curtain down on a lively stint behind the famous lectern that saw Leavitt repeatedly go viral for her clashes with the press.

From a two-word “your mom” comeback to fiery exchanges with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, here are some of her most memorable moments.

‘Your mom’

One of Leavitt’s cheekiest responses did not even come from the White House briefing room.



She went viral in October after sharing a text exchange with HuffPost White House correspondent S.V. Dáte as Trump prepared for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Hungary.

Dáte questioned the choice of Budapest as the proposed meeting place, pointing to its significance in relations between Russia and Ukraine.

“Does he not see why Ukraine might object to that site? Who suggested Budapest?” he asked.

Leavitt’s answer was short and sweet: “Your mom did.”



When Dáte questioned whether she thought the response was funny, Leavitt doubled down and branded him a “far-left hack who nobody takes seriously.

She added: “Stop texting me your disingenuous, biased, and bulls*** questions.”

Kaitlan clash

CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins also found herself on the receiving end of a Leavitt broadside during one heated White House exchange.

Collins challenged the press secretary in March over Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s criticism of media coverage of the deaths of American service members.



She claimed Hegseth was “complaining that it was front page news about these six service members who were killed.”

Leavitt immediately pushed back.

“That’s not what the secretary said, Kaitlan, and that’s not what the secretary meant,” she fired back.

“And you know it. You know you’re being disingenuous.”

Collins then read Hegseth’s full remarks and pointed out that news organizations report on US military deaths regardless of who occupies the White House.



But Leavitt wasn’t backing down.

“The press does only want to make the president look bad,” she said.

“That’s it. That’s a fact.”



‘Stupid question’

Another viral moment came during a June 2025 briefing when Leavitt was quizzed about Trump’s stance on demonstrations.

NOTUS reporter Jasmine Wright asked her to “clarify what kind of protest President Trump does support or find acceptable” after Trump issued a warning ahead of a military parade in Washington.

Leavitt replied that Trump “absolutely supports peaceful protests. He supports the First Amendment,” while stressing that “he does not support violence of any kind.”

Wright followed up by asking whether peaceful protests would be allowed on the day of the parade.

Leavitt appeared baffled that there was any doubt.



“Of course the President supports peaceful protests. What a stupid question,” she shot back.

Gulf row

Leavitt also went toe-to-toe with The Associated Press during a row that erupted over the newly renamed Gulf of America.

The Trump administration restricted the news agency’s access to some press events in early 2025 after the AP continued using Gulf of Mexico following Trump’s move to rename the body of water.

Leavitt defended the White House’s position as part of its push to hold news organizations accountable.

“It is a fact that the body of water off the coast of Louisiana is called the Gulf of America,” she declared.



The restrictions were later lifted.

But the AP found itself in Leavitt’s firing line again when reporter Josh Boak challenged Trump’s tariffs.

Boak asked why the president was “prioritizing tax hikes in the form of tariffs.”

Leavitt described them as a “tax hike on foreign countries,” prompting Boak to point out that tariffs are charged to importers.

That did not go down well.



“I think it’s insulting that you’re trying to test my knowledge of economics, and the decision that this President has made,” Leavitt responded.

Then came one final jab: “I now regret giving a question to The Associated Press.”

Leavitt will now swap the daily White House press battles for more time with her family, but she won’t be fully gone from Trump’s orbit.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The president has made clear he wants his outgoing press secretary close by as an outside adviser, meaning her headline-grabbing comebacks may not be over just yet.

News.title: Water bills set to rise for many after firms permitted extra funding
News.content:
Water companies have been given the green light to increase bills for customers by an extra Â£3.4bn in coming years to meet increased pressures on infrastructure and the environment.

Nearly a third of the extra funding provisionally approved for 13 water companies in England and Wales is earmarked for making sure water services are maintained.

Some of the rest will be used to meet rising demand from housebuilding and data centres and to address pollutants known as "forever chemicals".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the proposal was "real money out of family budgets at a time when they are struggling with the cost of living", and an environmental group described the decision as "an insult".

Customers of five water companies - Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, Thames Water, Wessex Water, and South East Water - are facing additional bill rises over the next two years, on top of increases that were already announced in 2024.

The new increases will vary between firms.

Southern, for example, will charge Â£43 extra next year, while South Eastern will only charge Â£1 more in 2029. The increases will only come into effect if they are given final approval later this year.

The other eight water firms identified - Anglian Water, Dwr Cymru Welsh Water, Hafren Dyfrdwy, Northumbrian Water, Wouth West Water, United Utiliites, Yorkshire Water, SES Water - would recover their additional spending through customer bills after 2030.

Many consumers are angry at being asked to pay anything more against a backdrop of interruptions to supply sometimes lasting for days, and rivers, lakes and beaches too polluted to use safely.

But water companies argue that these problems can only be solved by boosting spending to replace pipes, build treatment plants and establish new reservoirs.

Climate change has also increased pressure on the water infrastructure by making heavy rains and heatwaves more frequent.

News.title: Son pays tribute to dad, 102, who died after allegedly being assaulted in pub
News.content:
The son of a 102-year-old great-grandfather who died after allegedly being assaulted at a south Wales pub says he was a "pub character".

Phillip Ormerod, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, was taken to hospital in a critical condition following the incident at the Crow's Nest pub in the town on 1 August.

Gwent Police confirmed on Thursday that he had since died.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily harm, and remains under investigation.

Ormerod's son, Robert Ormerod, said his dad had been diagnosed with dementia and was a widower who lived alone.

News.title: The key signs you may have damaged your eyes by looking at the eclipse
News.content:
Eye experts are warning people to be on the alert for any signs their vision has been damaged by looking at the sun during Wednesday's eclipse.

The symptoms can include blurred vision, a central blind or dark spot and increased sensitivity to light.

After the previous total eclipse of the sun that was visible in the UK in 1999, around 70 people were left with damaged sight.

Many of them had spent less than a minute looking at the spectacle, without realising they were harming their eyes.

The danger comes because staring at an eclipse without protection can damage the retina, which sits at the back of the eye, and particularly those cells responsible for sharp central vision.

The sun is incredibly bright, even when partially obscured by the moon.

Normally if we stare at it, we wince and quickly look away.

But when it is darker, during an eclipse, that instinct may not kick in, even while our eyes are being damaged.

The bright light and ultraviolet radiation given off by the sun can lead to a condition known as "solar retinopathy".

And because the retina has no pain receptors, it's hard for people to notice the damage as it happens, so symptoms may only appear several hours later.

Leading up to the eclipse itself, experts were warning only genuine specially-designed solar eclipse glasses should be used, and that ordinary sunglasses or other devices were not enough to prevent potential damage.

News.title: Honeytrap thieves jailed for killing men they had drugged
News.content:
A couple who drugged men seeking sexual services in order to steal from them have been jailed for killing two men and poisoning others.

Adina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru admitted the manslaughter of Gary Mouat, 37, from Oxfordshire, and Malcolm King, 80, from Gloucestershire, in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

The pair also each admitted two further counts of administering poison to surviving victims on the first day of their trial in June.

Mihai and Dumitru were both sentenced to 17 years in prison at Oxford Crown Court.

Mihai, who posed as a sex worker, and her partner Dumitru, arranged to meet men paying for services she had advertised online at their homes.

The court heard four had their alcoholic drinks spiked with the powerful sedative gamma-butyrolactone (GBL) so the pair could steal from them.

Two men died as a result, while two others - who cannot be named due to reporting restrictions - survived.

News.title: Busiest ever period for England's A&Es as extreme heat hits
News.content:
England's A&Es are experiencing their busiest period ever, with the record-breaking heat cited as a key factor.

More than 2.4 million patients attended emergency departments each month for May, June and July â the three highest monthly totals recorded in history.

NHS bosses say the pressure has been as bad as it is in winter months. The extreme heat has caused people to fall ill with dehydration and heatstroke, and has increased the risk of complications for those with heart, kidney and respiratory problems.

It comes as unions warn staff are being forced to work in inhumane conditions because of the heat, with reports of some collapsing and others having seizures.

The problems have been further complicated by equipment, including scanners and IT systems, breaking down.

NHS medical director Prof Frankie Swords praised the "outstanding professionalism" of staff and said the situation was making delivering care challenging.

She advised: "With temperatures peaking today, please take sensible precautions to stay safe - keep hydrated, avoid the sun during the hottest part of the day, especially if you are clinically vulnerable, and check in on older or vulnerable friends, relatives and neighbours."

News.title: Voting under way in Clacton by-election
News.content:
Voting is under way in the Clacton by-election as a record number of candidates vie to become its next MP.

Fifty-one polling stations in the Essex resort, which includes the towns of Jaywick, Frinton and Walton-on-the-Naze, opened at 07:00 BST and will shut at 22:00.

An electorate of 79,785 registered voters have the chance to vote for one of 34 candidates - the most ever to stand in a British election.

Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to cast their ballot.

They will receive the longest ballot paper in British electoral history at 90cm - about 3ft long - to choose their candidate and cast their vote.

There are 12 political parties and 20 independents standing.

The constituency also has rural villages including St Osyth, Weeley and Great Bentley.

Polling stations will remain open to anyone registered to vote until 22:00, with the count taking place overnight.

News.title: Dating app Bumble divides users by ditching its signature 'women-first' chat rule
News.content:
Dating app Bumble has divided its users by dropping its signature rule which allowed only women to send the first message to a match.

When the app launched 2014, founder and boss Whitney Wolfe Herd said it distinguished itself from rivals like Tinder by allowing women to "make the first move".

But the thing that made Bumble famous will now be ditched following a trial which showed more engagement - and a survey among users which found 66% of women prefer men to send the first message.

Reaction across online forums has highlighted a divide among users about whether the update will get more people using Bumble - or if it makes it "just like any other dating app".

Previously, only same-sex relationships did not have to follow the strict women-first rule.

Another change coming to Bumble will extend the time-limit users have to initiate a conversation after matching.

Users will now have three days to begin messaging one another instead of 24 hours.

"While women making the first move was a radical idea, being women-first was never about prescribing just one way to connect," said Wolfe Herd.

"Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides."

In an April 2015 interview shortly after Bumble's launch, Herd Wolfe told the Toronto Star it was a "stereotype to say women like to sit back and want men to come to them".

News.title: Five key takeaways from results day 2026
News.content:
Results for A-levels, T-levels, BTecs and other vocational qualifications are out.

And this year, they've come at a time when all eyes are on what teenagers decide to do next.

Universities are keen to get them through the door. As they grapple with their finances, they know that every filled seat in a lecture hall comes with tuition fee funding.

The new prime minister, meanwhile, wants to carve out clear routes into technical jobs that can rival the well-established path of A-levels and a university degree.

For teenagers, considerations about the immediate and long-term cost of university, as well as the availability of other options, are all in the mix.

Here are the standout things you need to know.

News.title: Children in temporary accommodation hits record high
News.content:
Section 21 "no-fault" evictions, where tenants can be evicted without giving a reason, are widely regarded as a key driver of homelessness, and were banned from May 2026.

But Ronesha said "Section 21 is not the problem", adding: "My issue is the government allowing landlords to skyrocket rental prices, which are not in line with salaries.

"It doesn't add up."

The Labour government pledged to build 1.5 million new homes in England over the course of this Parliament, but is currently not on course to meet that target.

"It is shameful that a record number of children are growing up without a home because decades of political failure have choked off the supply of genuinely affordable social homes," said Sarah Elliot, chief executive of housing charity Shelter.

"Right now, too many children are spending their childhoods in temporary accommodation that is barely fit for a one-night stay, let alone years on end.

"Whole families are crammed into B&Bs, hostels and tiny bedsits that are freezing and damp in the winter and boiling in the summer."

In his incoming speech as prime minister, Burnham suggested the UK was in the grip of a "housing crisis" and that he wanted to deliver "the biggest council house-building programme since the post-war period".

Shelter said it wanted him to use October's Budget to "kickstart the council house revolution he promised" by removing financial barriers that prevent councils from building more social rent homes.

The total number of households in B&B accommodation fell by almost a quarter in the year to March, with the number of households containing children living in B&Bs falling by half.

About 1,000 households with children had been in B&B accommodation for more than the six-week limit, although this represented a fall on a year earlier.

"While it's welcome that more households are being helped into a home and fewer families are living in bed and breakfast accommodation, these figures show there is still a long way to go, with record numbers stuck in temporary accommodation," Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said.

The government has also pledged an additional Â£340m to end rough sleeping.

News.title: UK economy grows but experts warn of challenging months ahead
News.content:
Summer sun and sports fixtures helped the UK economy grow between April and June, according to official data, but some economists warned the outlook for the rest of the year was weaker.

The economy expanded by 0.4%, in line with market expectations but below a 0.6% increase in the first three months of this year.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said growth had "remained relatively robust", with the UK ahead of other G7 countries for growth this year so far.

Experts questioned whether this resilience would be maintained, however, given growth was fuelled by some temporary factors and energy prices could remain volatile if the Middle East conflict continues.

The British economy is now 1.2% bigger than a year ago, the ONS said, despite fears that the Iran war, which started at the end of February, and politically uncertainty around Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister would hold back growth.

Between April and June, sectors including computer programming, advertising and the pharmaceutical industry lifted growth. That was offset by falls in power generation and sewerage.

The ONS said some businesses reported that "good weather and sporting events may have had a positive effect" in June, boosting month-on-month growth to 0.3%.

The men's football World Cup, which kicked off mid-June, increased customers at hospitality venues showing the matches.

June also saw several of summer's heatwaves. However, May's growth was revised down from 0.1% to zero growth.

News.title: Harvey Nichols bought by owner of Sports Direct
News.content:
Luxury department store Harvey Nichols has been bought by the owner of Sports Direct, which warned a "significant restructuring" was needed to ensure the 200-year-old business remains sustainable.

Mike Ashley's Frasers Group will take control of the Harvey Nichols stores, including its flagship in Knightsbridge, as well as the international franchise.

The department store was immortalised in BBC sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, but had faced challenges in recent years. The firm had appointed administrators in June.

Michael Murray, Frasers' chief executive and Ashley's son-in-law, called the store a "British institution with significant potential" but added "clear meaningful change is needed".

"The turnaround will require tough choices and we are prepared to make those decisions, even if that means a smaller business in the near term, to create a stronger and more sustainable Harvey Nichols for the long-term," he said.

Harvey Nichols carries more than 800 premium and luxury brands and has over 1,000 employees. Its other stores are located in Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds and Edinburgh.

Frasers Group will also acquire the online business, and shops will continue to operate under their existing licensing.

Earlier this week, Harvey Nichols warned in its latest accounts that it would need to "cease trading" within a year if it failed to secure new investment.

It had faced "sustained trading and operational challenges" recently and Frasers Group said it will need to conduct a review of the store's portfolio, structure and cost base.

A recent auction for the store saw Frasers battle retail rival Next to take control of the firm.

Harvey Nichols was bought in 1991 by Hong Kong-based businessman Sir Dickson Poon but he put the group up for sale earlier this year.

News.title: Ski Sunday host Chemmy Alcott suffers collapsed lung after jumping into lake
News.content:
Ski Sunday presenter Chemmy Alcott says she suffered a collapsed lung after jumping into a lake while on holiday in France.

The 44-year-old former GB Olympic skier posted a clip on Instagram, external that showed her jumping off a five metre platform into Lake Annecy, in the French Alps, before landing badly and ending up in hospital.

"Most people badly time a front flip off a five-metre platform and get winded," she said in the clip.

"I apparently don't do things by halves. Collapsed lung, chest drain and a very expensive lesson in rotation."

Alcott explained that she initially went back to jump again after her difficult landing, out of "embarassment" and "just so I wasn't making a big deal out of it".

But she soon realised she "couldn't breathe properly and should probably go and get it checked out".

She later shared images of herself in hospital with tubes and wires sticking out of her body.

In the caption to the main clip - titled "this didn't end well" - she wrote: "Well... that escalated quickly. Turns out five metres is quite a long way to discover you've got the rotation wrong.

"One badly timed front flip. One very hard landing. One collapsed lung. One chest drain. And a few more hospital overnights than were on the holiday itinerary...

"I absolutely loved Annecyâ¦ but I'm not entirely sure it loved me back."

A collapsed lung - medically known as a pneumothorax - occurs when air becomes trapped in the space between the lung and the chest wall, according the NHS.

News.title: Met chief accepts mistakes made over Simon Levy but defends investigation into murders
News.content:
The head of the Metropolitan Police Sir Mark Rowley has defended the force's investigation into double murderer Simon Levy.

Levy was on bail and being monitored by police when he murdered Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins five months later, as well as violently raping a third woman.

Sir Mark acknowledged mistakes over the force's handling of Levy, but said suggestions it had not tried to build a case over his first murder were "just not true", following criticism including from Labour MP Jess Phillips.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that detectives had done "serious" work but "didn't have enough evidence" for a charge.

The Met did not seek a charging decision from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) over Valencia-Trujillo's murder until after Wilkins had been killed.

The police and CPS has apologised over a series of decisions that left the convicted sex offender free to attack the women.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is currently examining how Levy, 40, was managed over the four-year period from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, he was given a whole life prison sentence, meaning he will never be released.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark - who on Wednesday called the case a "whole system failing" - said he had already apologised for what the Met had got wrong.

It emerged after Levy's conviction that the Met did not class Valencia-Trujillo's death in March 2025 as a murder, or pass the case to specialist homicide detectives, until after he had killed again.

Sir Mark said "the public debate needs to be better informed" because "the facts on that are much more complex than people want to acknowledge".

He said that while Valencia-Trujillo's death was "clearly very suspicious and concerning", a pathologist was unable to determine a cause of death and the force "didn't have enough evidence to get to a charge".

Sir Mark added it was only after the murder of Wilkins that the Met had the "combined evidence" to move forward.

"So the inference that the Met didn't try on that case is just not true, the Met tried," he said.

However, the Met did not ask the CPS for advice about Valencia-Trujillo's death, let alone a charging decision, until after the murder of Wilkins, the BBC has previously reported.

The fact there was no formal cause of death would not have prevented the case being taken on by specialist homicide detectives, who are skilled at building murder cases even when there is not a formal cause of death.

Levy's semen was on Valencia-Trujillo and his blood was at the murder scene. CCTV that showed Levy in the area, walking in the same direction as Valencia-Trujillo shortly after she passed a camera, was not viewed by the local team despite being gathered.

Other possible relevant CCTV was never gathered, and had been deleted by the time the specialist murder team took over months later.

In that case, the local team investigating the death did not engage with the Met's specialist murder teams apart from the day her body was discovered in March 2025.

A specialist homicide team attended the crime scene that day and recommended the case stay with local officers pending further enquiries, but there was no further contact until after Wilkins was murdered in August.

News.title: Boy suffered fatal brain injury in seaside drowning
News.content:
A seven-year-old boy suffered a fatal brain injury after he got into difficulty off the Essex coast, a coroner has said.

Musa Ahmed died six days after the incident in West Mersea, in which his 15-year-old cousin, Sameeha Rahman, and her mother, Shelina, 41, also died.

They were all enjoying a day out to the island, near Colchester, from east London when the tragedy unfolded on 22 July.

Their provisional causes of death were all given as drowning at an inquest opening in Chelmsford, while Musa also died from a hypoxic ischaemic brain injury.

"Clearly it is so tragic to come across the death of any individual," said Lincoln Brookes, the senior coroner for Essex.

"But when three occur at the same time and all from the same family, one cannot understand the tragic nature of such an incident."

Three others were taken to hospital by ambulance after the incident and are said to be recovering.

News.title: XL bully dog which fatally bit man was not type to savage anyone, defendant says
News.content:
Fong appeared visibly upset as she spoke of her relationship with Keven Jones, describing him as her "father-in-law", although she was not married to his son.

She said she got on with him "really well", describing him as a "functioning" drug addict who was anything "you would expect a normal person to be".

He had owned several dogs during his life, including a boxer and a "Bully breed" at the time of his death, she said.

On the morning of the incident, she said Jones was outside the house when she heard him say: "Get off me Cookie, or get off me mate."

She sobbed as she was asked if she had control of the dogs at the time or saw what was happening, repeatedly saying: "No."

She continued crying as she recalled dialling 999 and was instructed how to perform CPR by the operator.

"I remember shouting to the paramedics that they needed to hurry up... I was scared... it was horrible."

Asked why she later agreed to euthanise Cookie, she said: "Because it was the right thing to do."

Cross-examined by the prosecution, she was asked whether she had made any effort to establish if Jones had taken drugs or had any concerns about him taking charge of the dogs.

"I never knew when he was or wasn't on drugs," she said.

"You didn't bother to ask him?" she was asked by Connor, responding: "No."

She was also repeatedly asked if she had become complacent about the dogs or underestimated the danger they represented.

She replied: "I did underestimate him because he did what he did."

The trial continues.

News.title: Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplant failings
News.content:
While NHS Blood and Transplant manages organ donations and supports transplant centres, services are commissioned and paid for by NHS England.

But in a letter to NHS England and a small group of patient advocates, Manas said the central body had created a "fragmented" system "with poor accountability".

There is a "mismatch", he said, between each hospital's waiting lists, organ availability, capacity to carry out surgeries and the availability of operating theatres.

This is "leading to last-minute cancellations [and] unpredictable utilisation of donated organs," he warned.

The BBC reported in March that the UK, once a world leader, had fallen behind major Western nations in heart and lung transplantation, though it fares better in other areas such as kidney transplantation.

The NHS transplants one in 10 lungs and one in seven hearts that are donated - half the proportions seen in some other countries.

It has not invested in modern technology at the same rate as other countries, and suffers from a lack of theatre space, intensive care beds and staff.

Wales and Northern Ireland do not have a heart and lung transplant centre, so patients commonly travel to England for surgery. There is one heart transplant centre in Scotland.

News.title: Tommy Robinson’s ex-wife denies failing to comply with accounting rules as trial date set
News.content:

Tommy Robinson's former wife has denied allegations that she failed to comply with corporate financial record-keeping regulations.

Jenna Lennon, 41, pleaded not guilty to three counts of failing to adhere to company accounting rules at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday.

Andrew Evans, prosecuting on behalf of the Insolvency Service, said the charges pertain to "various books and records offences" involving Hope & Pride Limited, a business where Lennon "was formerly the sole director".

Dressed in a black trouser suit, Lennon was released on bail by His Honour Judge Tony Baumgartner ahead of a further case management hearing on October 1 2026.

A trial date has been set for July 31 2028.

Lennon denied failing to surrender books and records to a liquidator between September 22 2023 and December 1 2025, contrary to the Insolvency Act 1986.

open image in gallery Lennon was previously married to Tommy Robinson ( PA Wire )

She also denied failing to ensure that the company kept adequate accounting records between September 18 2020 and September 19 2023 under the Companies Act 2006.

Lennon further denied failing to preserve corporate financial records over that same period, also contrary to the Companies Act 2006.

Robinson and Lennon married in 2011, but divorced in February 2021. They have three children together.

Robinson recently issued a surprise apology to a Muslim student who was targeted by an aggressive online hate campaign after a viral clip of their Oxford Union debate was taken out of context.

The controversial debate in mid-June focused on the motion "This House believes the West is right to be suspicious of Islam."

Robinson, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, spoke in support of the motion, alongside Reclaim Party founder, Lawrence Fox, and Times of Israel journalist, Jonathan Sacerdoti. They lost the debate.

A clip circulating online after the debate was published on YouTube late last week, showed Aisha Khan-Aziz, a student speaker delivering the first speech for the opposition, introducing the speakers on the side opposite to her by making a joke about each of them, as per union tradition.

Introducing the former English Defence League (EDL) co-founder, Ms Khan-Aziz said: “Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known to his hooligans as Tommy Robinson.

“Stephen, there is a crowd outside rioting against you tonight, and without the protection and generosity of a Muslim Palestinian president and a largely South Asian executive committee, you would be quite literally cooked."

The comments are widely understood to have emphasised the commitment of ethnic minority groups to freedom of expression.

While Robinson congratulated the opposition during the debate, the release of the clip has seen Ms Khan-Aziz face a litany of abuse on X. The Oxford student is accused of threatening the EDL leader with violence by supporters of the far-right.

But in a surprise move last week, Robinson took to social media, issuing an apology to Ms Khan-Aziz for allowing her words to be “taken out of context and weaponised.”

Admitting that there was no “Muslim mob” outside the university, Robinson added: "So I apologise Aisha, if you're watching this. I apologise, because I know you didn't mean that.

“And I should have spoken up from the first minute, but I was too interested in point scoring on the side of us against Islam, which is a w****r move because I know you didn't mean it."

Oprah Winfrey has addressed her part in platforming the careers of pro-Trump doctors Dr. Phil McGraw and Dr. Mehmet Oz on her titular talk show.

Winfrey’s The Oprah Winfrey Show show aired from 1986-2011. She introduced McGraw — who is no longer a licensed psychologist after letting his license lapse two decades ago — as a weekly expert and relationship strategist in 1998. Oz, who holds medical and business degrees from the University of Pennsylvania, began appearing on the program as a medical expert in 2004.

Both TV doctors have since become allies of President Donald Trump and his MAGA movement.

McGraw, AKA Dr. Phil, serves on Trump’s Religious Liberty Commission and promotes MAGA initiatives through his conservative cable network Merit Street Media and accompanied ICE agents to a raid in Chicago with his TV network in June 2025 for a “first-hand look at the target operations.”

Oz was appointed to lead the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in 2025, and has consistently supported Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again agenda.

open image in gallery Oprah Winfrey (left) invited TV personalities Dr Phil McGraw (center) and Dr Mehmet Oz (right) on her eponymous daytime talk show in the early aughts ( Getty Images )

In a new interview with Emmy Magazine, Winfrey admitted that she faces criticism for having platformed the pair because of their current political views, but was defensive about why she chose them to join her show in the first place.

“Everybody has their own path in life, and it has not one thing to do with me, and I don’t have one thing to do with them,” she said.

“At the time, the reason and intention behind me giving them their breaks was I thought they had valuable information to share that had been meaningful to me,” she continued.

Winfrey praised McGraw for supporting her during a 1997 lawsuit, where she was sued by a group of Texas cattlemen for defaming the beef industry. She won the case in February 1998.

“He was so practical, so down to earth, so real,” she said of McGraw. “He would ride in the car with me every morning on the way to trial, where I’m literally sitting on trial for six weeks.”

Winfrey said her best friend Gayle King introduced her to Oz.

“He explained practical things like colon cancer and bowel movements,” Winfrey said. “I thought he had the language for explaining medical things in a way that was helpful to me. I thought it would be helpful to many other people. And that is how they ended up on the show.”

While Winfrey and Trump were on friendly terms before he became president, she publicly endorsed Kamala Harris during the 2024 election and delivered a speech at the Democratic National Convention.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump pictured in 2025 alongside Dr. Phil McGraw, who serves on Trump’s Religious Liberty Commission ( Getty Images )

open image in gallery Trump works closely with Oz, who serves as Administrator for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services ( AFP/Getty )

Both McGraw and Oz’s medical expertise has been scrutinized by health professionals over the years.

At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, McGraw faced backlash for suggesting social distancing was unnecessary and sharing inaccurate statistics about non-contagious causes of death.

“The fact of the matter is we have people dying, 45,000 people a year die from automobile accidents, 480,000 from cigarettes, 360,000 a year from swimming pools, but we don’t shut the country down for that,” McGraw said on Laura Ingraham’s The Ingraham Angle.

McGraw has previously said he sends a letter to Winfrey each year to express his gratitude for their friendship and how it changed his life.

“Oprah and I met in the late ‘90s when she was on trial, and I was on the trial team, then I started doing the show, and started doing the show a lot,” he said on The Kelly Clarkson Show in 2022. “And then we launched the [Dr. Phil] show, and it really changed my life a lot.”

“I had a great life when I met her, and I’ve got a great life now, but she changed a lot of things,” he said.

CNN Senior Political Contributor Scott Jennings has shared an update on Senator Mitch McConnell’s “private” health battle, saying that he “seemed to be doing a lot better.”

The conservative pundit told his CNN colleagues on Tuesday’s episode of The Arena With Kasie Hunt that he talked with the Kentucky Republican on the phone earlier in the day.

“He left the rehab facility several days ago, and he's been recovering at home,” Jennings, McConnell’s former political director and longtime friend, told a panel hosted by Pamela Brown filling in for Hunt. “I could tell being at home was better than being in the hospital.”

McConnell has not been seen in public since early June after taking a fall that landed him in the hospital. He was subsequently moved to a rehabilitation center, from which he was discharged on Thursday.

open image in gallery CNN Senior Political Contributor Scott Jennings has shared an update on Senator Mitch McConnell’s health battle, saying that he ‘seemed to be doing a lot better’ ( Reuters/Mitch McConnell’s office )

When CNN contributor Lulu Garcia-Navarro asked Jennings why McConnell was talking to him and not calling into media outlets with updates, he said the senator is a private man.

“My belief about males of that generation is that they're intensely private,” Jennings, who is also from Kentucky, said. “He's always been a little private about his own personal healthcare.”

McConnell, a survivor of childhood polio, has suffered from a series of falls and public episodes of freezing up in recent years.

In October, McConnell fell in a hallway inside the U.S. Capitol building as he was approached by an activist asking him about Immigration and Customs Enforcement activities.

open image in gallery Jennings said McConnell has ‘always been a little private about his own personal healthcare’ ( Getty Images Courtesy of the Rainey Center )

The senator’s office has only provided a few written statements and photos from McConnell in recent weeks, fueling baseless conspiracy theories that the 84-year-old had died and his team was covering it up.

When McConnell released a photo of him and his wife, Elaine Chao, in the hospital last month, some accused the photo of being fake, specifically mentioning the Washington Post’s Sunday sports section that the senator was holding.

But the publication verified that the photo was not AI-generated.

In his most recent statement, McConnell said, “On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business.”

open image in gallery Jennings said he believes McConnell is hopeful of getting back to Capitol Hill by September 14 ( Reuters )

The senator also said he and Chao were grateful for the outpouring of support he has received from friends, colleagues and constituents and the “attentive care” he’s received from medical professionals.

Jennings said he believes McConnell is hopeful of getting back to Capitol Hill by September 14, when the Senate returns from its August recess.

McConnell, Kentucky’s longest-serving senator, is not seeking reelection and will retire next year.

“There's an election in Kentucky in November. He'll be out of office come January,” Jennings pointed out. “So this is the last few weeks of the Senate session of his term.”

India’s viral “cockroach” youth group has signalled a new phase of mobilisation days after their massive Gen Z-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.

Speaking at a gathering of volunteers in the capital Delhi on Wednesday, Cockroach Janata Party founder (CJP) Abhijeet Dipke alleged that his group had been prevented from holding a planned meeting at a banquet hall under pressure from the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Mr Dipke said he planned to return with the movement after its 36-day agitation at Delhi's Jantar Mantar was called off on 25 July.

"Many people were commenting on Instagram when Season 2 of 'Jantar-Mantar' will begin. I want to tell them that Season 2 of 'Jantar Mantar' is going to start very soon,” he said, referring to the protest site in Delhi.

Mr Dipke said the party had struggled to find a venue for a volunteers' meeting, with several hall owners allegedly refusing to rent their premises.

open image in gallery Abhijeet Dipke, founder of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), addresses celebrating supporters following the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, after days of protests demanding he step down over the alleged Neet examination paper leak scandal on 25 July 2026 ( Getty )

"We were scheduled to hold our volunteers' meet in Delhi today. We were looking for a hall, but no one would rent us one. Everyone kept saying there was pressure from above (government)," Mr Dipke said.

He claimed the group eventually secured a venue, only for its owners to receive threats on the morning of the meeting.

Mr Dipke accused prime minister Narendra Modi’s BJP of being behind the intimidation. The Independent has reached out to the BJP for comment.

open image in gallery Supporters of India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) queue up for free pizza sent by unknown supporters through food delivery apps ( Reuters )

But he said the alleged attempts to disrupt the meeting had helped the movement.

"The more they go against us, the more it works in our favour. They're unable to understand how to deal with us,” he said.

"Today also they thought if they threaten the banquet hall we won't hold the meet. Now the closed door meeting has become a public event. I think they want a Jantar Mantar everywhere," Mr Dipke added.

The CJP's original Jantar Mantar protest was centred on the alleged paper leak of a key undergraduate medical entrance exam and demands concerning education.

It ended after the then federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned and the government agreed to the protesters' other key demands – including assurance of no police action against them.

The demonstration had drawn students and young volunteers from across India, as well as opposition leaders.

Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk joined the protest on 28 June and later began an indefinite hunger strike before being taken to Safdarjung Hospital in the city when his health deteriorated.

open image in gallery Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) chant slogans and wave their mobile phones with their flashlights on ( Reuters )

The group has since sought to broaden its campaign beyond the original protest.

Its chief spokesperson, Saurav Das, said it was beginning a nationwide "listening tour" to hear from the public, with education among its first priorities.

"This itself is Season Two. Protests are taking place across the country against such incompetent governments and officers. On behalf of CJP, we are now embarking on a nationwide 'listening tour' to hear what the public has to say. We will run a campaign, and we are prioritising the issue of education starting from Independence Day."

Mr Dipke said Wednesday's meeting had been intended to discuss support for a student-led agitation in the eastern state of Jharkhand.

"Ranchi protest is led by Devendra Mahto, who is sitting on a hunger strike. Our volunteers are supporting. Today we were going to discuss how to strengthen the Jharkhand agitation, and how to continue our campaign for schools in villages," he said.

The group has also called on village heads and parents to improve basic facilities in government schools, including electricity, water, toilets and midday meals. Dipke has urged parents to document deficiencies and said the CJP would launch a form to collect information on school infrastructure.

The UK is now in the midst of its fifth heatwave of the year and on track to be the hottest summer on record.

Temperatures hit 37C on Thursday and provisional Met Office data shows the UK’s mean temperature for meteorological summer so far is currently at 16.48C – that is 1.88C above the 1991 to 2020 average temperature.

England has recorded a mean summer temperature of 18.19C so far, 2.46C above average. The remainder of August would need to be 1.41C below the summer average for England to equal its current warmest summer on record, also set in 2025.

Persistent dry and hot weather is taking its toll on England and Wales with about 70 per cent in drought.

Following a record dry July and very low levels of rain at the start of August, 27 million people are now under water-use restrictions.

But will this be the last heatwave of the summer? Or is there another dry and sunny spell looming over the UK?

open image in gallery The Uk is currently in its fifth heatwave of the year ( PA )

What does the long range forecast say?

The Met Office long range forecast shows high pressure may start to weaken next week bringing the potential for some showers or longer spells of rain. But temperatures are still expected to be slightly above average.

However, towards the end of the month, high pressure is predicted to return, which is likely to bring back longer periods of dry weather and warm temperatures and maybe even another heatwave.

"Looking ahead, forecasts indicate temperatures will remain well above average through much of the coming week, with another spell of heatwave conditions expected to develop in some areas,” Met Office senior scientist Mike Kendon said.

“While individual hot spells do not determine seasonal records on their own, sustained periods of warmth throughout the summer have contributed to the exceptionally high average temperatures we've seen so far,” he added.

That means the UK could see another heatwave, which would bring the total for the year to six.

open image in gallery England has recorded a mean summer temperature of 18.19C so far, 2.46C above average

What records have been broken this summer?

The Met Office said on Thursday afternoon temperatures had reached 37.6C at Charlwood in Surrey, while at Wisley temperatures had hit 37.2C, and Kew Gardens in London had recorded a temperature of 38.1C – the highest temperature recorded in the UK this year.

A further 10 weather stations were at or above 36C, the provisional figures from the Met Office showed.

It makes 2026 the first year on record to see three separate days where temperatures reached the 37C threshold, as well as the first year with four days at 36C or above.

Before 2026, the UK had recorded 37C or higher on only six occasions.

It also extends 2026’s record-breaking run of days above 35C.

For four months in a row temperatures hit 35C in the UK on at least one day in May, June, July and now August.

July was also the driest month since records began in 1836 in both England and Wales, southern England alone had its driest calendar month ever on record.

By 15 July this year the UK had already recorded more days above 30C than in the whole of 1976, which was known for its long-lasting heatwave.

News.title: ‘More pain’ to come after economic slowdown
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The economy grew at a slower pace in the second quarter of the year, official figures show, under pressure from the Iran war.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc between April and June, down from 0.6pc in the first three months of the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.

The figures underline the challenge that the conflict poses for Andy Burnham, who has pledged to deliver “growth in every postcode”.

The Prime Minister has already been warned that the economy will slow further next year if Donald Trump continues his war in the Middle East.

Treasury officials have predicted UK growth of just 0.3pc in 2027 if the Strait of Hormuz stays blocked for the rest of this year.

That is far lower than the 1.6pc predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March, based on assumptions made before the start of the war. Here is what you need to know.

Asian shares were mostly higher, powered by gains for AI-related stocks including computer chips as regional markets tracked a rally on Wall Street.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 advanced 1.6pc to 68,601.21. In South Korea, the Kospi jumped 4pc, climbing to 6,844.65, as shares in Samsung Electronics surged 5.4pcc. Computer chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 7.1pc.
