Lagos, Nigeria’s economic juggernaut, would not be quarantined from the fallout. A destabilized South West would trigger capital flight, disrupt supply chains and send the already battered naira into a death spiral. The 1967 crisis taught the country that what begins as a regional political feud can, within months, engulf the entire federation.

The run up to the Osun governorship election is already ringing alarm bells. Political rallies have become avenues for violent clashes. Intelligence reports indicate that non state actors, including militia groups from neighbouring states, are being mobilised under the guise of providing electoral security. There are credible fears that federal agencies could be deployed not to protect voters but to sway outcomes. A replay of the local government poll carnage, in which several persons were shot dead and ballot materials were brazenly hijacked, would be catastrophic at the governorship level. If such events occur and Davido activates his promised Washington pipeline, the consequences cascade rapidly.

First, the United States would likely impose targeted sanctions, including visa bans and asset freezes, on individuals identified as electoral violators. These measures would not discriminate between party affiliations; any Nigerian official, from the state resident electoral commissioner to ministers deemed to have orchestrated interference, could be hit. The families of such individuals, many of whom school, bank and own property in America, would find their lives upended overnight.

Second, the amplified international scrutiny would paralyse Nigeria’s diplomatic capacity to negotiate vital economic agreements. The World Bank and International Monetary Fund, already cautious about Nigeria’s fiscal trajectory, would face renewed pressure from Western capitals to attach strict governance benchmarks to any support.

A country that cannot conduct a credible state election cannot credibly ask for debt relief or investment guarantees.

Third, and most dangerously, the security landscape would deteriorate. A perception that the presidency has stolen another South West state after what the opposition describes as controversial outcomes in previous cycles would radicalise a generation of young voters.

Davido’s fan base, numbering millions of largely urban, digitally connected youths, would transform from passive consumers of Afrobeats into an angry, mobilised constituency. Protests may erupt not just in Osun but in Lagos, Ibadan, and the diaspora capitals. In a nation where the #EndSARS movement demonstrated how quickly a local incident can ignite a global conflagration, adding a Trump angle would make any crackdown instantly transnational. The Nigerian military and police, already straining under a global human rights microscope, would find themselves exposed to fresh sanctions and reduced foreign training support.

President Tinubu stands at a crossroads that will define his legacy. As a founding figure of the National Democratic Coalition, he once risked his life fighting military dictatorship precisely to install the democratic order now under threat. His entire political biography is built on the principle that civilian government must be superior to the tyranny of rigged mandates. When he ordered the EFCC to unfreeze the Osun bank accounts, he demonstrated that he possesses the instinct to check overreach by his own appointees. That single decision earned him plaudits from civil society, the international community, and even his fiercest critics. It was the act of a statesman who understands that the office of the president is the custodian of national cohesion, not a party secretariat’s bludgeon.

That same courage is what the Osun governorship election now demands. The President must instruct the Inspector General of Police, the Department of State Services, and all paramilitary agencies to remain absolutely neutral. The Independent National Electoral Commission must be given the political space to function without the usual pressure to deliver a predetermined winner. Security personnel who collude with political thugs must face exemplary prosecution. State resources, including the army of federal government officials descending on Osun for “official assignments,” must not be converted into a parallel campaign structure. The judiciary, too, must resist the impending temptation to adjudicate electoral disputes through the prism of political loyalty rather than law.

There is no patriotic argument for rigging an election in a democracy already precariously balanced on a knife edge.

The political rewards are fleeting and poisoned. Even if federal might secures the governorship seat today, it would govern a shattered state filled with embittered citizens, international isolation, and an opposition that will never recognise its legitimacy. The economic cost of such a pyrrhic victory would obliterate any gains. Investors who already view Nigeria as a high risk environment need only read a U.S. government sanctions list to retract their commitments. The Nigerian diaspora, a multibillion dollar lifeline through remittances, would face added banking friction as compliance departments tighten rules on transactions linked to politically exposed persons.

The path forward is clear and entirely consistent with the President’s own “Renewed Hope” agenda. Nigeria’s developmental ambition, to lift 100 million citizens out of poverty, to become a $1 trillion economy, to lead the African Continental Free Trade Area, cannot be achieved without political stability.

Political stability, in turn, cannot coexist with electoral banditry. Every stolen mandate shortens the horizon for economic planning. Osun State, with its expanding agricultural potential, its vibrant small and medium enterprise sector, and its strategic position in the South West economic corridor, needs a governor with the untainted mandate to pursue an audacious development agenda. That governor must emerge from a transparent process that, even in defeat, the loser can accept without unleashing chaos.

President Tinubu can author the script for that outcome. He can convene a meeting of all Osun political stakeholders, not to dictate terms but to issue an unambiguous public assurance that Abuja will not be a partner to any electoral crime. He can direct the National Security Adviser to establish a special election security monitoring unit that reports directly to the presidency, bypassing compromised political gatekeepers. He can invite international observers, including the European Union and the African Union, well in advance, and grant them unfettered access. Most powerfully, he can make a national address in which he stakes his personal honour on the integrity of the Osun poll, promising that anyone in his government found interfering will be sacked and prosecuted, no matter their rank.

Such steps would not only neutralise Davido’s Trump threat but turn the election into a showcase of democratic maturity that attracts, rather than repels, foreign partnership. The United States, instead of probing anomalies, would be citing Osun as evidence that Nigeria is finally turning a corner. The Afrobeats industry, led by its most influential son, would transform from potential whistleblower to national cheerleader.

A Plea from History

The dead of the Wild Wild West did not get the chance to plead with their leaders. They were consumed in fire set by political arsonists who believed they could control the blaze. The three million who perished in the civil war that followed never imagined that a regional political feud would morph into a national graveyard. Nigerians alive today, navigating the daily trauma of inflation, insecurity and joblessness, are pleading silently that history not be repeated.

President Tinubu, by ordering the unfreezing of Osun’s bank accounts, has already shown he can hear those pleas. The coming Saturday’s governorship election is his opportunity to prove that Nigeria’s democracy, under his watch, has truly graduated from the primitive era of rigging and violence into a mature system where votes count and mandates are sacred. If he resists the temptation to interfere, he will be remembered as the leader who prioritised nation over party, stability over power, and posterity over expediency. If he falters, the consequences, amplified by a global pop icon and an American president looking for Nigerian scalps, will be too severe for the country to bear.

The safe election way forward is not a secret. It is the application of the same principle that restored Osun’s bank accounts: respect for the rule of law. Let the people choose. Let their will stand. Nigeria’s economic development, its political advancement, and its very survival as a forward looking sovereign nation depend on it.

-Dr Akinfosile writes from Lagos.

World.title: Coastal town where you can buy acres of land for R200 000
World.content:
South Africa’s coast is vast. Yet living by the coast is still considered a luxury.

Often, buyers think they’ll need millions.

But you can get on the property ladder on South Africa’s coast for as little as R200 000.



In one coastal town, you can get acres of land for next to nothing. But is it worth it?

The Coastal Town where Land is Affordable

Hibberdene on KwaZulu-Natal’s south coast is the town where you can get affordable land. Large portions of Hibberdene are unspoiled and still undeveloped.

According to a listing on Property24, one real estate agent is selling 18 parcels in a development for R200 000.



However, the 1.9 hectares (4.6 acres) comes with conditions.

The buyer only has rights to develop the plots until 2038.

The development, made up of timber-frame homes, is 1.3 kilometres from the beach.



Rates and levies total R3 244 a month.

Buyers will likely have to pay this on each lot they buy, a R58 392 monthly expense for 18 plots.

Other properties in Hibberdene don’t have these conditions and don’t come with these kind of rates and levies.



The starting price for a 976-square-metre plot is R150 000.

A 1 693-square-metre plot in Catalina Bay goes for R180 000. Rates are more reasonable at R100 a month.

Value along KwaZulu-Natal’s South Coast

The rest of KwaZulu-Natal’s south coast still has some affordable land.



Town Land Size Price Range Hibberdene 684 m² – 7.2 ha R130 000 – R2.7 million Marina Beach 949 m² – 6.5 ha R185 000 – R3.2 million Trafalgar 1 317 m² – 7 404 m² R117 500 – R4 million Port Edward 584 m² – 5.8 ha R100 000 – R53 million

Prices along the South Coast

Although coastal buyers want the sweet salty scent of the sea, they also want access to amenities, city amenities.

Location is important.

Beyond views, South Africans care about roads, services, safety, and community.



The Western Cape has long been considered the go-to province for coastal living.

The Garden Route, Cape Town, and now the West Coast stand out as the biggest winners.

Each of these areas offers buyers amenities and safety.



However, prices have been steadily rising for years as demand increases.

Currently, getting a plot of land within 100 kilometres of a major Western Cape town will set you back at least R300 000.

Some buyers are shifting focus to other coastal provinces and considering getting in on the ground floor.



KwaZulu-Natal is one such option.

But market values don’t always reap positive returns for buyers.

In Hibberdene, prices dropped 20% in four years.

Area 2021 Average 2025 Average Difference (%) Hibberdene R650 000 R520 000 -20% Marina Beach R762 500 R895 000 17.5% Trafalgar R490 000 R900 000 83.7% Port Edward R727 500 R685 000 -5.8%

There are also gems in the Eastern Cape, Western Cape, and Northern Cape where buyers can get land for between R200 000 and R300 000 minutes from the beach.



Areas like Quigney in the Eastern Cape or Lambert’s Bay in the Western Cape are such areas.

Quigney’s average home price in 2024 reached R595 000 according to Property24.

By 2025, it was R850 000, a 43% increase.

As of 2026, those gains are being lost.

To date, the average home price in the region is R650 000.



Although you can find a home in Lambert’s Bay for less than R600 000, the town’s average price as of 2026 is R1.3 million.

This is a 56% rise from the average 2025 price of R850 000.

These kinds of price increases make the area out of reach for many.



That’s when the South Coast can become appealing.

World.title: Bafana Bafana starlet swaps English football for MLS
World.content:
Bafana Bafana and Queens Park Rangers (QPR) starlet Tylon Smith has officially signed a season-long loan deal with Major League Soccer side New England Revolution.

Smith, who was touted as South Africa’s next biggest superstar in England, is joining New England Revolution through the 2027 MLS Sprint Season.

New England Revolution said in a statement that they have an option to make Smith‘s stay permanent at the end of his loan deal.



Also read: South Africans Abroad: Mbokazi ruled out for the rest of 2026

BAFANA BAFANA STARLET SMITH MOVES TO MLS

“The New England Revolution have acquired central defender Tylon Smith on loan from Queens Park Rangers F.C. through the 2027 MLS Sprint Season, with an option to purchase,” reads part of the statement.

“Smith, 21, arrives in New England following a brief spell with Queens Park Rangers F.C. of the English Football League (EFL) Championship, where he suited up for 10 appearances across the senior and U-21 levels from 2025-26. Prior to QPR, Smith began his professional career with his hometown club, Stellenbosch FC of the South African Premiership, after developing through the club’s academy.”

Also read: Former PSL superstar finds new home in North Africa!

WHAT NEW ENGLAND REVOLUTION CHIEF SAID ABOUT SMITH…

“Tylon Smith is a promising player who will help strengthen our defense,” Revolution General Manager and Chief Soccer Officer Chris Tierney said.

“At just 21 years old, Tylon has built a strong foundation through both his club and youth national team experience. We’re confident that this is the ideal environment for Tylon to continue his development and we look forward to welcoming him to New England.”

World.title: Pensioner loses home and belongings in KZN fire
World.content:
Reaction Unit South Africa officers assess the scene after a fire destroyed a 74-year-old woman’s home in Buffelsdraai, KZN. Image: Supplied by RUSA

A 74-year-old woman lost her one-room home and all her belongings after a fire destroyed her residence in Buffelsdraai, KwaZulu-Natal.

Reaction Unit South Africa (RUSA) received a call for assistance at about 21:07. When Reaction Officers arrived at the scene, they found the home completely destroyed.

The pensioner was unable to save belongings

The elderly woman told officers she lived alone and had been visiting a neighbour when she heard a loud explosion. She rushed outside and saw her home engulfed in flames.



Neighbours tried to put out the fire, but their efforts were unsuccessful. The woman could not save any of her belongings, including her identity documents and bank cards.

Allegations of possible arson

The woman claimed that a neighbour had confronted her during a meeting last Thursday and accused the pensioner of practising witchcraft.

She believes the fire may have been deliberately started after the dispute. However, the allegation could not be immediately verified.

No injuries were reported.

World.title: Former PSL superstar finds new home in North Africa!
World.content:
Former PSL and Mamelodi Sundowns superstar Lucas Ribeiro Costa has finally found a new home in North Africa.

On Thursday, African football powerhouse Esperance Sportive de Tunis announced the acquisition of Ribeiro Costa.

Ribeiro Costa had been linked with a number of African clubs after becoming a free agent at the end of last season.



The left-footed attacker then signed on the dotted line with Libyan giants Al-Ittihad Tripoli but he has since moved to Esperance.

He had a change of heart soon after the departure of coach Rulani Mokwena who was instrumental in bringing him to Libya.

Ribeiro Costa joins Esperance on a three-year deal in a swap deal that will see Jacques Diarra move in the opposite direction.



Also read: Sundowns in talks to secure loan move for fringe goalkeeper!

FORMER PSL SUPERSTAR LUCAS RIBEIRO COSTA JOINS ESPERANCE

“Last night, the vice president of the Tunisian sports club Esperance, Shakeri Al-Wa’ar, traveled to Libya to complete the procedures for the transfer of the Brazilian player Lucas Ribeiro to our club,” reads the statement.

“This morning, a meeting was held with a delegation from the Tunisian sports club, led by Shakeri Al-Wa’ar, and a delegation from the Libyan club, led by the executive director Abdelmajid Saleh, to finalize all the arrangements for this process.



“This is thanks to the Tunisian sports club, headed by the club president, Mr. Hamdi Madab, and his brother from the Libyan club, the Union of Libya, for their warm reception and treatment, which paves the way for further strengthening of relations and cooperation in the coming phase.”

Also read: Mngqithi outsmarts Barker to lift first trophy in Tanzania

IS THIS THE PERFECT MOVE FOR LUCAS RIBEIRO COSTA?

Let us know in the comment section below…

World.title: PowerBall Xtra’s cascade clock is ticking again
World.content:
PowerBall Xtra has rolled over three times since its last cascade on 31 July 2026: Image ChatGPT

Twice now, Sizekhaya’s PowerBall Xtra cascade rule has turned an unwon jackpot into guaranteed millionaires.

A third cascade is already on the way, and here’s exactly when to expect it.

Two cascades down, one more guaranteed

On 30 June 2026, a R139 million PowerBall Xtra jackpot cascaded down to three winners, who each walked away with R45 733 457.30.



On 31 July 2026, the rule triggered again, this time paying R23 810 456.50 to a single player who matched the five main numbers without the bonus ball.

Since that second cascade, PowerBall Xtra has already rolled over three times.

Friday, 14 August’s draw now sits at R12 million.



Why the timing actually matters

Sizekhaya’s cascade rule guarantees PowerBall Xtra pays out on the final draw of every calendar month, no matter what.

Friday, 14 August is only the fourth PowerBall Xtra game of the month, so this cascade point is still a few draws away.

Counting rollovers won’t change your odds on any single draw, since every number combination carries identical odds regardless of when you play.



But it does tell you exactly when a guaranteed payout is coming, which is useful if you’re deciding when to get a ticket in.

What’s changed since Sizekhaya took over

The main PowerBall jackpot odds have actually improved under Sizekhaya, shifting from 1 in 42 million to 1 in 33 million after the number pool shrank.

PowerBall Xtra carries identical odds to the main draw, since it uses the same number matrix.



Eish, I’ll be honest, hey, I don’t play by counting rollovers myself. But knowing Sizekhaya locks in a guaranteed payout by month’s end definitely makes the final PowerBall Xtra draw of August one to watch.

Would knowing a cascade is guaranteed make you more likely to play the final draw of the month?



The South African is the first to deliver Daily Lotto, Lotto and PowerBall results each day. Check back at 21:00 for tonight’s results.

World.title: All Blacks mix and match with team selection for Bulls clash
World.content:
Taylor will captain the All Blacks for the first time in his 110th All Blacks match, and in what will be his first match of the tour, against the Bulls. Props Xavier Numia and Tyrel Lomax will also play their first match of the tour.

Six players from the All Blacks team who beat the Sharks 54-0 on Tuesday retain their places in the matchday 23 for the Bulls match: lock Josh Lord, loose forward Wallace Sititi, halfbacks Kyle Preston and Cortez Ratima (who are both playing their third game of the tour), midfielder Timoci Tavatavanawai, and outside back Emoni Narawa.
