World.title: Quarter-Century After Peace Deal, North Macedonia Has Yet to Fully Heal
World.content:
The anniversary comes at a time when Ohrid is again at the centre of political debate.

The Democratic Union for Integration, DUI, the main ethnic Albanian party that was formed by the former leaders of the insurgency, and has been in government for much of the time since the conflict ended – before being relegated to the opposition after the 2024 general elections – has accused the current VMRO DPMNE party-led government of undermining the agreement.

It has pointed to several developments.

These include challenges to the constitutionality of the Law on the Use of Languages, opposition to bar exams being taken in Albanian, the abolition of the so-called “Balancer” mechanism for ensuring equitable ethnic representation in public employment – and a current push to adopt an new Law on Fair and Equitable Representation, designed to replace the “Balancer” system.

Popetrevski, however, doubts a coordinated government plan to dismantle Ohrid. “I see no basis for claiming that there is a coordinated plan to dismantle the Framework Agreement,” he says.

“After 25 years, it is not only legitimate but necessary to reassess how the solutions stemming from the Framework Agreement are functioning,” he adds.

The “Balancer” system illustrates the dilemma. Introduced to help ensure equitable representation of ethnic communities in public institutions, it achieved much of its intended purpose, Popetrevski says – but also produced “absurdities”, such as cases of people changing their declared ethnic identity to obtain employment.

The language law, he adds, also should not be beyond scrutiny, particularly given the concerns raised by the Venice Commission over aspects of its implementation, including the broad use of bilingualism in court proceedings.

At the same time, Popetrevski cautions against ignoring the cumulative effect of several contentious issues being raised within a short period.

“Politics does not happen in a laboratory, in an isolated system,” Popetrevski says. If questions concerning language, equitable representation and the Badinter mechanism are raised simultaneously, this may create an impression among some Albanians “that there is a step backwards from 2001”.

That is why, he argues, any changes to the deal must come with a clear political message.

“If dysfunctional solutions are being corrected, it must be unequivocally clear that the constitutional fundamental values and principles are not being called into question,” he asserts.

At the same time, Popetrevski rejects the DUI’s claim that is the sole “guardian” of Ohrid. “The DUI has no exclusive right to interpret and defend the Framework Agreement,” he insists.

A party that spent almost two decades in government, he argues, also bears responsibility for the agreement’s shortcomings.

“If every criticism of a particular solution is declared an attack on the Framework Agreement, then the agreement is transformed from a mechanism for building cohesion into a tool for day-to-day political mobilization,” he says.

Popetrevski’s assessment is also shaped by his own recollections of 2001.

Aged 25, he was reporting for one of the country’s national television stations when the conflict erupted. Covering a war in his own country while attempting to maintain journalistic distance was one of the most difficult professional challenges of his career.

“In a conflict, nuances are very easily erased. Either you are ‘ours’ or you are ‘theirs’,” he recalls.

In an article several years ago, he wrote that those in his newsroom who managed to be “journalists first and Macedonians and Christians afterwards” were a minority. He stresses that this was not a criticism of his colleagues, but a reflection of the atmosphere of the time.

A quarter of a century later, he believes distance has made those lost nuances easier to see.

“There was genuine dissatisfaction among Albanians with their position in the state. Acknowledging that does not mean justifying the taking up of arms,” he says.

The reverse is equally true, he adds: condemning the use of weapons does not mean denying that serious problems existed before the conflict.

“Perhaps the most important thing we know today is that there was no military solution,” he assesses.

The wider international context was crucial. The United States and European Union opposed any redrawing of borders, even though partition and territorial changes were among the ideas circulating during the conflict.

Beyond simply ‘not shooting each other’

World.title: Romania Shuts Nuclear Reactor on Danube as Power Crisis Deepens
World.content:
Romania shut down its last operating nuclear unit on Thursday as record-low Danube water levels threatened the cooling system at the Cernavoda nuclear power plant, adding to concerns over electricity supplies during a prolonged heatwave.

The shutdown leaves both reactors at the country’s sole nuclear plan offline. Cernavoda normally accounts for about 20 per cent of Romania’s electricity production.

Officials say the closure will not significantly affect Romania’s energy situation.

“Shutting down the last reactor is a controlled process that will only last about 10 days … during this time, Romania will have the resources to cover the energy deficit in the grid,” Romeo Urjan, director of the Cernavoda plant, said.

The Energy Ministry in a statement said higher wind power production is expected, while a coal-fired power unit is also due to restart.

Authorities are also preparing to increase electricity imports, mainly from neighbouring Bulgaria and Ukraine, to maintain supplies and avoid disruption, as demand remains high in the extreme temperatures.

The government has already urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption during peak evening hours until the end of the month, to ease the pressure on the power system during the ongoing heatwave.

More than 80 large industrial consumers have either reduced production or scheduled maintenance to cut electricity use, while restrictions have also been imposed on water use for agricultural irrigation.

The exceptionally low Danube levels have affected river transport, tourism and the energy sector. The government declared a nationwide energy alert on July 31, which will remain in force throughout August.

The energy crisis has also fuelled a surge in conspiracy theories and fears that Romania could face a nationwide blackout. Energy experts, however, doubt such a scenario.

“People have no reason to fear; they will not be left without electricity. Romania will resort to imports when necessary … though these will be more expensive because all countries in the region need electricity during the same evening peak hours,” energy analyst Corina Murafa said.

Murafa warned that higher electricity costs for consumers could be a likely consequence of the situation, as Romania relies more heavily on imports while domestic nuclear generation remains suspended.

While the shutdown at Cernavoda is not expected to last long, continued heat and low Danube levels could keep pressure on the country’s energy system for some weeks.

World.title: Turkey Targets Major Religious Group With Organised Crime Charges
World.content:
Turkish police detained Alihan Kuris, leader of one of Turkey’s largest religious groups, known as the “Suleymancilar,” and 48 others on Thursday as part of an investigation into an alleged organised crime group.

The Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office said detention warrants had been issued for Kuris and 48 other suspects as part of an investigation into alleged offences.

They include establishing and managing a criminal organisation, membership of a criminal organisation, laundering proceeds of crime, fraud against public institutions and violations of tax law.

“The criminal organisation sought through this method to prevent access to company records and make it more difficult to trace financial transactions,” the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement.

It said a report by Turkey’s Financial Crimes Investigation Board, MASAK, found that many companies linked to the suspects had recorded significant increases in financial transactions and purchases and sales since 2020.

Prosecutors alleged that a number of the companies subsequently underwent divisions and transfers, while new companies were established with large amounts of capital, sometimes in different provinces and operating in sectors unrelated to the original companies.

The investigation targets one of Turkey’s largest religious communities.

The so-called Suleymancilar are inspired by Turkish imam and preacher Suleyman Hilmi Tunahan, who was originally from Bulgaria and died in 1959. The group’s main focus is Koranic education and it runs thousands of dormitories, cultural centres and other facilities in Turkey and abroad, particularly in Germany.

The group opened a part of its new headquarters in Cologne in recent weeks with some financial support from the German government.

Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci said Kuris, Tunahan’s maternal great-grandson. took over the movement in 2016, after which its activities began to be conducted with greater secrecy.

“They are building a large centre in Cologne, Germany. We assess that once this building is completed, all of their activities will be moved there,” Ciftci said, describing Thursday’s operation as one targeting the organisation’s financial network.

The group is also known for its political and business activities. It controls an extensive network of companies and business interests, amounting to a sizeable business empire with activities spanning construction, food production and publishing, among others.

Former group leader Arif Ahmet Denizolgun was Turkey’s transport minister in the 1990s, as a member of the centre-right Motherland Party.

His nephew, Arif Ahmet Denizolgun, was an MP for President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, from 2018 to 2023. Denizolgun is at odds with Kuris’s leadership.

The group has never enjoyed particularly close relations with Erdogan’s AKP, however, as it has traditionally opted to support centrist parties rather than political Islamist parties.

Following the failed coup attempt in 2016 and the subsequent crackdown on the so-called Gulen movement, which the Turkish authorities accused of orchestrating the coup attempt, some Islamist circles urged action against the Suleymancilar.

In Turkey’s 2023 general election and 2024 local elections, the group reportedly supported opposition parties against Erdogan’s ruling alliance.

World.title: ‘Absurd Blockade’: Fresh Parliamentary Deadlock Pushes Kosovo Back Into Crisis Mode
World.content:
This Tuesday, Avni Dehari entered Kosovo’s parliament – but not for the task he is formally entrusted with.

The 79-year-old MP from the ruling Vetevendosje party is parliament’s provisional speaker, as its oldest member, tasked with moderating the inaugural session of the Assembly until MPs vote on a permanent speaker.

Parliament is stuck again in apparent deadlock, with Dehari’s party refusing to submit a name for the speaker, as it first demands an agreement with other parties on the election of a new President of Kosovo.

Parliament’s rules require him to invite the MPs to a session every 48 hours until they elect a speaker.

But the last time Dehari actually presided over a session was last Saturday, August 8, and that session lasted only a few minutes.

World.title: Albania Gambles on Re-Legalising ‘Dangerous’ Online Sports Betting
World.content:
When the Albanian government finalised its ban on gambling in 2019, the official narrative promised to uproot a social scourge that had spread to almost every street corner in Albania. At the time, there was hardly a neighbourhood without two or three betting shops.

Street betting shops and online gambling were banned, while casinos were restricted to certain upscale hotels.

Seven years later, the Albanian government is preparing to legalise online sports betting once again, although it had continued operating informally despite the ban.

Following the adoption of the law by parliament to re-legalise in 2024, the Ministry of Finance told BIRN that all secondary legislation has now been approved and that the regulatory framework is considered complete.

“The system is legally ready, but the licensing process has not yet officially opened,” the ministry said in a written response.

World.title: Political Deadlock in Romania Threatens €770m EU Lifeline
World.content:
An unusual meeting on Tuesday afternoon between Romanian President Nicusor Dan, government representatives and leaders of the main pro-European parties was visibly tense from the outset.

Political leaders were not smiling, not even as a matter of protocol. Their greetings were formal, as was their interaction throughout the meeting. The talks were important because they were expected to adopt a law that would allow Romania to avoid losing approximately 770 million euros in funding from the EU-backed National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

European funds are vital to Romania’s strained budget, supporting healthcare, education and infrastructure projects. EU funding is equivalent to around one third of the country’s gross domestic product. Romania must reform its public sector law in order to receive the EU’s funding.

Yet the meeting ended without any concrete result.

World.title: Kosovo Probes Alleged Police Violence Against Serb During Raid
World.content:
North Mitrovica Hospital , Kosovo, where the man received treatment. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s Police Inspectorate said on Wednesday that it was investigating reports published on August 11 claiming officers used excessive force against a Serb man, Nenad Raskovic, during a raid at his home near the northern municipality of Zubin Potok.

Photographs shared on media and social networks show injuries on Raskovic’s back.

The Police Inspectorate, IPK, said it had interviewed Raskovic at North Mitrovica Hospital, where he is receiving treatment.

“The IPK has initiated this preliminary investigation with the aim of verifying the allegations and clarifying all relevant facts and circumstances related to the case,” the Inspectorate, an independent institution overseeing police conduct, said in a statement.

The Inspectorate said it would take all necessary steps, including “cooperating with relevant institutions, obtaining official documents and information, and interviewing people who may have knowledge of the incident”.

The Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party, Srpska Lista, said Raskovic said police officers entered his home in Dren village on Tuesday and, after searching the property, began hitting him without explanation.

“After that, Nenad was left tied to a tree. With the help of friends, he was freed and taken to the Family Medicine Centre in Zubin Potok, and then to the Clinical Hospital Centre in Mitrovica,” the party said.

In interviews given to media from hospital, Raskovic alleged that he was beaten by Kosovo police.

The Srpska List party called on Western embassies and organisations, NATO-led peacekeepers in KFOR and the EU rule-of-law mission EULEX to “examine the allegations and take action within their respective mandates to establish the facts and ensure the rights and safety of citizens”.

Petar Petkovic, head of the Serbian government’s office for Kosovo, also posted photos of the alleged injuries inflicted by Kosovo police on Tuesday, saying that “these are photos of [Kosovo Prime Minister Albin] Kurti’s ‘democracy’.

“For weeks, months and years, we have been warning the entire international community about the persecution of Serbs by Kurti’s regime, which has led to this. When those responsible face no sanctions and there is no adequate protection, these are the consequences,” Petkovic wrote.

Kosovo Police confirmed searching Raskovic’s home. Erduan Baliqi, a police spokesperson for the North Region, told BIRN: “Raskovic’s house was among the properties searched during the operation in Dren village… The searches were related to information on weapons.”

Baliqi said the police had “no information about the use of violence”.

Civil society organisations in Serb-majority northern Kosovo have called on the European Union to assess EULEX’s monitoring of the Kosovo Police.

“These allegations require an urgent and independent investigation, as well as an appropriate response from the relevant institutions,” they said in a statement.

The allegations come as attention focuses on war-related crimes in the Zubin Potok area, where excavations have been carried out in several villages in search of mass graves.

So far, remains believed to belong to four people have been exhumed, while three people have been arrested on suspicion of war crimes against civilians.

World.title: Croatian Tourism Minister Says Last Minute Bookings are Saving August
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – The Croatian tourism minister has stated that last minute bookings are saving August, with more and more people paying closer attention to value for money before making reservations.

Croatian tourism is once again confirming its strength this year, and the results achieved show that we are on the right track, said Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the month of July’s tourism results were better than expected, and indications suggest that the second half of the summer could follow the same pattern.

According to data from the eVisitor system, which records tourist traffic in commercial and non-commercial facilities as well as nautical charters (eCrew system), Croatia recorded 12.4 million arrivals and 59.1 million overnight stays from January to the end of July. Compared with the same period last year, this represents growth of 1 percent in both arrivals and overnight stays.

Of that total, 56.1 million overnight stays were recorded on the Adriatic (up 0.5 percent year-on-year), while the continent, including the city of Zagreb, recorded more than 3 million overnight stays (up 1 percent).

july was fantastic for croatia

eVisitor data also shows that in July this year, Croatia recorded 4.7 million arrivals and 29.6 million overnight stays, which is an increase of 2.5 percent in arrivals and 1 percent in overnight stays compared with July last year. In the seventh month the most guests came from the markets of Germany, Slovenia, Croatia, Poland, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary and others. By counties, the most tourists were counted in Istria, Split-Dalmatia County and Kvarner, while the most visited destinations were Rovinj, Vir, Poreč, Medulin and Dubrovnik.

“We are satisfied with the tourism results achieved in the first seven months of this year, and especially with the fact that in July we recorded the best result of the last two years. This confirms that Croatian tourism continues to maintain its competitiveness and resilience and that, despite changes in the market, we are succeeding in maintaining positive trends. We are particularly pleased that good results are also being recorded in financial indicators.

In July the value of fiscalised invoices rose by 18 percent, while the number of issued invoices was 8 percent higher than in the same month last year. Growth is also being recorded in road, air and maritime traffic, and all these results confirm that we have responded well to market circumstances – both through quality promotion of Croatia and through timely adaptation of the offer. I thank the entire tourism sector for the effort invested, and especially accommodation providers who responded to our appeals and, with their promotional offers, additionally contributed to the competitiveness of our offer.

Ahead of us is still a good part of August, after which we will make a complete overview of this main part of the tourist year. Croatian tourism is once again confirming its strength this year, and the results achieved show that we are on the right track and that together we are successfully responding to changes and challenges,” said Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport.

When Croatia’s tourism results are broken down by counties, in the first seven months the most overnight stays were recorded in Istria (16.7 million), Split-Dalmatia County (11.1 million) and Kvarner (9.7 million), while by destinations the leaders were Dubrovnik, Rovinj, Poreč, Split and Umag.

last minute to the rescue

“The course and results of the tourist year so far show that Croatia still has a very strong position on the global tourism market, despite all the demanding circumstances. What we particularly read from this year’s tourist movements is a change in the way guests make decisions about their trips. Last-minute bookings play an important role, and when choosing a destination, the best value for money is increasingly sought, along with safety and easy accessibility. In this context Croatia has a series of advantages – from proximity to our most important source markets and good transport connections to the diversity of the offer that enables different types of holidays.

Given the considerable number of promotional last-minute arrangement prices in August, the tourism sector believes that the August figures will also be good.

The results achieved therefore give us additional wind in our sails for the continuation of the tourist year, all the more so because the Ferragosto period is ahead of us, traditionally very important for travel by Italian guests. In addition to the main summer months, we are also recording excellent advance bookings for the shoulder season, for which promotional activities begin in mid-August, especially on the Polish and UK markets,” said Kristjan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board.

Looking at markets, during the first seven months the most overnight stays were recorded by guests from Germany (10.3 million), Croatia (7.6 million), Slovenia (6.7 million), Austria (4.3 million), Poland (3.9 million), the Czech Republic (3 million), the UK (2.2 million), Hungary (2.1 million) and others.

Given the considerable number of promotional last-minute arrangement prices in August, the tourism sector believes that the August figures will also be good, at least at last year’s level.

59.1 million overnight stays were recorded over the first seven months of this year

Interesting trends can also be seen on individual markets. Thus eVisitor figures show that Croatian tourism in July and during the first seven months of 2026 recorded significant growth in tourist traffic from the Czech, Hungarian and Italian markets.

The most pronounced positive shift was recorded on the Czech market. Compared with July last year, the number of arrivals of Czech tourists rose by 12 percent, while the number of their overnight stays was higher by seven percent. In the period from January to the end of July growth of five percent was recorded in both arrivals and overnight stays compared with the same period last year. The Hungarian market is also a reason for satisfaction. During July the number of arrivals of Hungarian tourists increased by eight percent, while the number of overnight stays rose by seven percent.

In the first seven months of the year growth of seven percent was recorded in both arrivals and overnight stays compared with last year. Hungarian guests stayed most on Kvarner, in Istria and Zadar County. The Italian market, which had stagnated in recent years, is also recovering. In the period from January to July the number of arrivals and overnight stays of Italian guests increased by two percent compared with the same period last year, while in July a one-percent growth in arrivals was recorded.

World.title: Croats are Travelling Less and Taking Less Annual Leave This Summer
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – Croats appear to be travelling less and taking less annual leave this summer, with the latest research into these habits showing a marked change.

Almost every third person in Croatia is staying at their usual place of residence this summer, primarily due to a lack of financial resources, according to a survey conducted by Alma Career Croatia. Poslovni reports that the results of the latest survey on annual leave, carried out by Alma Career Croatia, an international company best known for the MojPosao/MyJob portal, show that Croatian employees are planning their holidays a little more cautiously this summer.

According to this latest survey, Croatian workers enjoy an average of 25 days of annual leave, and summer is the period when most employees use the largest part of their free days. However, this year’s results show that habits are slowly changing.

shorter summer breaks

Compared with 2025, the number of workers who plan to use fewer days of annual leave during the summer is rising, as is the number of those who aren’t planning on taking any trips at all this year.

The share of employees who plan to use a maximum of seven days of annual leave has increased from 15% in 2025 to 21% in 2026. On the other hand, the share of those planning to rest for 21 days or longer has almost halved (7% last year, 3% this year). The most common choice remains a holiday lasting 8 to 10 days, planned by 37% of respondents. This is followed by those who will rest between 11 and 15 days (29%), while 10% of employees plan annual leave lasting between 15 and 20 days.

The issue with summer that is becoming increasingly problematic is the fact that the weather is becoming so insufferably hot that sitting under the air conditioner is the only choice for a growing number of people. Most can do that at work or at home.

the croatian coast still dominates for most croats, as opposed to heading somewhere abroad

When it comes to destination, Croatia remains the first choice.

More than half of the survey participants (56%) plan to spend their summer holiday within the country, which is only slightly less than last year, when the figure was 58%. There are also somewhat fewer people planning a trip abroad this summer. Their share has fallen from 21% in 2025 to 17% this year.

However, the biggest change is visible among those who do not plan to travel at all. Their share has risen in one year from 27% to 32%, meaning that almost every third respondent will not go on a summer holiday this year. Finances are most often behind such a decision. Among respondents who will not travel, as many as 60% cite lack of financial resources as the main reason, compared with 56% last year.

One to two weeks on the Adriatic; shorter or longer holidays abroad

There are also differences in the length of holidays depending on whether respondents holiday in Croatia or travel abroad. Those who holiday somewhere else within Croatia most often choose a classic break of one to two weeks. As many as 78% of them plan to rest between 8 and 15 days.

People who travel abroad more often choose either very short or significantly longer trips. Thus, 21% of respondents travelling outside Croatia plan a holiday of seven days or less, while among those staying in Croatia the figure is 10%. At the other end of the spectrum, 7% of travellers abroad plan a holiday longer than three weeks, while among those holidaying in Croatia only 2% plan such a break.

World.title: Adidas Strengthens Presence in Croatian Sport as Cibona Signs Partnership
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – Adidas is strengthening its present in Croatian sport as the famous Cibona signs a partnership deal with the global sport brand.

As Poslovni reports, one of the most successful Croatian basketball clubs of all and one of the most recognisable global sports brands are joining forces, and Cibona’s players will compete in adidas kit from the new season.

The global sports brand Adidas and Basketball Club Cibona, one of the symbols of Zagreb and Croatian sport, have officially begun a new collaboration. From the 2026/2027 season, Cibona’s senior and junior teams will compete in Adidas sports equipment.

The new partnership connects two brands deeply rooted in sporting history, yet simultaneously oriented towards the future, the development of new generations of athletes and the creation of top conditions for their work and progress. adidas will provide Cibona with modern sports equipment designed to give players maximum comfort, freedom of movement and the best possible performance on the court.

Founded in 1946, Cibona has over eight decades grown into one of the most important institutions of Croatian basketball. The club reached the peak of European glory in the mid-1980s when, led by Dražen Petrović, it won two consecutive European champion titles – in 1985 and 1986. After Croatia’s independence, Cibona won a record 20 national championship titles, and in 2014 it also won the regional ABA League.

“Collaboration with Adidas represents an important step in the development of the club for Cibona and a confirmation of the values that our club has carried for eight decades. We’re connecting with a global brand that understands sport, excellence and the importance of creating new generations of players. We believe this partnership will further strengthen our sporting identity, as well as the bond with the fans who have always been an inseparable part of Cibona. We look forward to everything we’ll achieve together on and off the court,” said Tomislav Šerić, director of Basketball Club Cibona.

The collaboration between Cibona and Adidas is part of the brand’s broader commitment to basketball, sport and athletes at all levels. Basketball is one of Adidas’s global sports categories, alongside football, running and training, while the brand is also active in tennis, golf, motorsport, winter sports, rugby, cricket and numerous other disciplines. For more than 75 years Adidas has been developing products intended for athletes, combining innovation, design and experience gained in professional sport.

“We are extremely pleased that Cibona is becoming part of the adidas sports family. This is a club of exceptional tradition, whose name holds a special place in the history of European basketball and which for generations has been home to top players. We share a belief in the power of sport, the importance of working with young people and a constant drive for progress. We’re extremely proud to support Cibona’s players with equipment that combines sporting innovations, functionality and the recognisable Adidas design, and we look forward to jointly creating a new chapter in the club’s history,” said Petra Franić from Adidas.

The partnership between adidas and Cibona opens a new chapter in the life of a club that placed Zagreb at the centre of the European basketball map. The recognisable three stripes will thus accompany the Wolves from the new season on the path towards new sporting successes.

Players of KK Cibona have for the first time completed a training session in the new training kit from the collection, while the official match kits will be presented later. The kits and selected items from the collection will be available to fans exclusively in the Basketball Club Cibona fan shop.

World.title: Danube Traffic Collapse Could Stretch into September and October
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – The current Danube traffic collapse could end up stretching into autumn as contracts worth 800 million euros fail.

Convoys with goods are stuck in front of the Mohovo Channel upstream from Ilok and as many as 60 Danube voyages have been postponed. Marija Brnic reports for Poslovni that over recent days in Vukovar, all eyes have been firmly fixed only on the forecasts of the State Hydrometeorological Institute and the numbers on the local water gauge. Since measurements of the Danube water levels began, it has never been lower, and in recent days it has almost completely halted river traffic in Croatia’s largest river port.

For two weeks already there have been practically no berthings of cargo barges or tourist cruise ships, and the critical point is the Mohovo Channel near Šarengrad, where the depth of the fairway does not meet the minimum conditions for safe and financially viable transport.

The crisis is entering its third week, yet what is worrying is that there are no good news in sight for its end. For August it is certain that regular traffic will not resume, even if heavier rain falls, and concern is also growing about September and even October. The Port of Vukovar has already put forward the first estimates of possible losses.

the port of vukovar is struggling

One topic is how to close natural retention areas by installing weirs, and the other issue that needs to be opened is the cleaning of the Danube along its entire course. With partners, as company director Marijan Kuprešak explained, they had contracted the transhipment of around 200,000 tonnes of various goods over the next three months. At an average transhipment price of 4 euros per tonne, this means the collapse of valuable contracts and a loss of around 800,000 euros in revenue. The scale of the potential damage in such a worst-case scenario is illustrated by the fact that this is somewhat below the level of revenue the company achieved in previous years; last year it stood at 1.2 million euros.

This year was expected at the Port of Vukovar to be a year of recovery from the crisis the company has been going through, largely due to the war in Ukraine and the associated reduction in traffic. At the current depth of the Danube, ships have to sail with reduced capacity, and apart from meaning that more voyages are needed for the same quantity of cargo, there is also the risk of grounding or the cost of ships standing idle, which currently makes this form of goods transport uncompetitive.

Until now it was precisely the lower price that gave river transport an advantage over road or rail. Kuprešak says that truck transport, which users are largely opting for in such situations because of investments in the railway, is several times more expensive than river transport.

Business partners, Kuprešak says, still show understanding, but if the drought continues, because of the dynamics of their own contracts and deliveries they will be forced to divert cargo to trucks and trains, which will of course spill over further onto their costs and the final prices of products. According to available information, cruise ships are also not docking in Vukovar and around 60 contracted voyages have been cancelled, mostly from Germany, for which the paid money has been refunded. The companies have suffered a loss of business of around one million euros per voyage.

Companies can as a rule recover any losses only through insurance companies, and even if a state of natural disaster were declared, previous practice shows that the state does not cover such damage outside the agricultural sector. However, Kuprešak says that at the level of shipowners, ports and landing stages of the countries all directly affected by the Danube water-level crisis, discussions are beginning about a possible initiative to seek assistance through horizontal support from the European Commission.

Non-repayable subsidies at that level would help, he says, to cover the losses that everyone will be hit by this year, but as climate change increasingly affects the European area and impacts rivers, an equally important issue that the state and the EU need to address is securing the navigability of the Danube. And that, Kuprešak says, is becoming increasingly threatened.

“One topic is how to close natural retention areas by installing weirs, and the other issue that needs to be opened is the cleaning of the Danube along its entire course,” Kuprešak stresses.

1 million euros in losses have been suffered by the companies that organise voyages on the Danube.

issues impacting croatia from germany to romania

In some countries, they have already carried out blasting and dredging to ensure passage at bottlenecks, but because of the extreme drought and record-low water levels, which appear to be becoming an increasingly pronounced problem in these areas, the issue will have to be approached more systematically and cover the entire course of the Danube, from Germany to Romania.

Blasting and the removal of underwater rock masses as well as deepening the riverbed is a permanent solution also for the Mohovo Channel, because it is the most sensitive point in the Croatian section of the Danube. For many Croatian companies the functioning of the Danube and the Port of Vukovar is an important business link, and among the users are numerous agro-combinates, producers of artificial fertilisers, cement and bulk cargo for the construction industry.

Until now the Danube was considered a navigable waterway 365 days a year, and a problem would at most appear because of ice in the winter months, but now the risk is becoming the summer period and drought. Shipowners, ports and landing stages therefore also see the historic drought affecting the Danube and river transport as an opportunity to sound the alarm in Brussels for the launch of a comprehensive, strategic regulation of the Danube and the permanent securing of its navigability.

World.title: Accommodation Owners Claim Croatian Local Host Campaign Started Late
World.content:
August the 12th, 2026 – The Croatian Tourist Board is satisfied, but accommodation owners are claiming that the Croatian Local Host campaign started too late.

“We’re extremely satisfied with the results of the first Local Host label campaign,” stated Kristjan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ). Croatia very successfully recorded 12.4 million arrivals from the beginning of the year to the end of July.

Ana Roksandic/Poslovni reports that eight million impressions and almost 500 completed reservations are the results of the first joint promotional campaign by the Croatian National Tourist Board and the Booking.com platform dedicated to Croatian family accommodation and hosts gathered under the Croatian Your Host/Local Host label.

The campaign “Experience real Croatia” ran during the months of June and July on the markets of Germany, Austria, Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary. At its heart were the actual local hosts themselves and the authentic experiences they offer their guests, the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) announced.

room for improvement

So far, over 3,570 properties with over 21,170 beds have joined the Croatian Local Host project. The largest number of properties with the Local Host label are located in Istria, on the Kvarner and in Split-Dalmatia County. Looking by destination, the highest numbers are in Crikvenica, Dubrovnik, Pula, Rovinj and Medulin.

“All of our activities are aimed at protecting genuine family accommodation that has been building Croatian tourism for generations and giving special value to our tourism offer. These hosts are precisely the foundation of Croatian tourism, which is why their protection will continue to be our focus,” revealed Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport, adding: “For the first time, we ‘ve also carried out a national promotional campaign dedicated exclusively to family accommodation, and the first results are already visible through 6 percent better occupancy, which confirms that the market recognises the value of authentic hospitality.”

the coast, of course, dominates the campaign

The largest number of properties with the Local Host label are situated in Istria, on the Kvarner and in Split-Dalmatia County.

As HTZ stated on its official website, the “Your Host” (Local Host) label enables hosts to stand out among numerous private accommodation providers and reach guests looking for an authentic and hospitable experience. Label holders can also use the official Local Host visual identity, and their offer can be included in HTZ promotional activities on foreign markets and digital channels. The label also provides them with guidelines for further raising the quality and sustainability of their business. However, among family accommodation providers there are also questions about the criteria for obtaining the label and its real impact.

“In fact, this label tries to make a distinction between such hosts and landlords where the guest often has no contact with the host at all. They arrive, get a code for the key, enter the apartment and leave, and you practically don’t even know who stayed in your accommodation. When you have the Local Host label, you should be present in the place where the property is located. Not necessarily at the address itself, but you should live, or have your residence, in that town or place. If, for example, you rent out a holiday home in Šibenik-Knin County and live in Split, you will not be able to get that label, regardless of the fact that you are available to the guest in that holiday home.

The reason is that your address of residence is not in the municipality or city where the property is located. Obviously there is still a little room for fine-tuning there, but there are people who already have that label and who work exactly like that – they are truly present and available to their guests,” said Ante Glavaš, vice-president of the Croatian Association of Family Accommodation (HUOS), adding: “However, some people in residential buildings have also received these labels. On what principle that happened is not clear to us.”

has this label led to higher occupancy rates?

HTZ says the label leads to higher occupancy: “In addition to an initially higher occupancy rate, properties that are part of the Local Host programme in 2025 recorded further positive progression: their occupancy grew by 5.74 percent compared to the previous year, while the occupancy of properties that are not part of the programme grew by only 0.6 percent. In the first five months of 2026 the occupancy of properties that are part of the Local Host programme, both in absolute terms and in terms of growth rate, remains higher compared to properties that are not in the programme relative to the same period of the previous year.”

However, one label holder we spoke to said the campaign did not have a particularly promotional effect on her property because it was carried out during June and July. Olinka Gjigaš, director of the Tourist Board of the City of Križevci and holder of the “Your Host” label in the Municipality of Kalnik, stressed that she is speaking from personal experience about the campaign’s impact: “I can’t really say there were any changes because the campaign started quite late. At the time when the promotion was being filmed, I already had 90 percent of the dates booked. I saw that the minister spoke about six percent growth, which surprised me – I wonder how that was even calculated.”

HTZ, however, rates the campaign results significantly more positively. “We’re extremely satisfied with the results of the first Local Host label campaign on the Booking.com platform, as well as with the overall effect of the promotional activities aimed at this label so far,” said Kristjan Staničić, director of HTZ, adding that the Local Host project is continuously gathering an ever larger number of hosts. HTZ will continue promotional activities in the second half of the year, when a new wave of the campaign on the domestic market will follow from mid-August to the end of October.

5.74 percen is how much the occupancy of Croatian Local Host properties grew compared to last year, which arguably isn’t much.

istria takes the lead

In a broader context, the Local Host results come at a time when Croatian tourism has been constantly recording a positive continuation of the season. According to data from the eVisitor and eCrew systems, from the beginning of the year to the end of July Croatia recorded 12.4 million arrivals and 59.1 million overnight stays, which is one percent more than in the same period last year. On the Adriatic 56.1 million overnight stays were recorded, or 0.5 percent more, while on the continent, including Zagreb, more than three million overnight stays were recorded, with growth of one percent.

In July alone, 4.7 million arrivals and 29.6 million overnight stays were recorded. Compared to July last year, the number of arrivals increased by 2.5 percent and the number of overnight stays by one percent. The most guests came from Germany, Slovenia, Croatia, Poland, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary.

Istria retained its leading position among the counties with 16.7 million overnight stays in the first seven months, followed by Split-Dalmatia County with 11.1 million and Kvarner with 9.7 million overnight stays. Among destinations, Dubrovnik, Rovinj, Poreč, Split and Umag lead.

World.title: June Sees Drop in Overnight Stays in Croatian Commercial Accommodation
World.content:
August the 12th, 2026 – June saw a drop in overnight stays in Croatian commercial accommodation recorded, with Istria County outperforming the rest of the country.

A mixed picture could be garnered when looking at overnight stays realised in Croatian commercial accommodation facilities in June this year. Jutarnji reports that a total of 3.0 million tourist arrivals and 13.5 million overnight stays were recorded. Compared to June 2025, tourist arrivals were down by 6.6% and overnight stays by 6.1%, according to the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS).

the germans (of course) lead the way

Of the total overnight stays realised, domestic tourists accounted for 8.9% and foreign tourists for 91.1%. Domestic tourists recorded 387 thousand arrivals and 1.2 million overnight stays, which is 11.8% more arrivals and 11.7% more overnight stays than back in June 2025. Foreign tourists recorded 2.6 million arrivals and 12.3 million overnight stays, which is 8.9% fewer arrivals and 7.5% fewer overnight stays than back in June 2025.

The highest number of overnight stays realised by foreign tourists in June 2026 was achieved by tourists from Germany, totalling 2.7 million overnight stays, or 22.1% of all foreign overnight stays. Compared to June 2025, their overnight stays were down by 28.1%. On average, they recorded 7.7 overnight stays per arrival.

After German tourists, the largest shares of foreign overnight stays were held by tourists from Austria (10.3%), Slovenia (9.9%), Poland (8.8%), the Czech Republic (6.6%), the United Kingdom (5.3%) and Italy (3.8%). Compared to June 2025, increases in overnight stays were recorded by tourists from Italy (5.0%), Slovenia (3.9%), Poland (3.2%), the Czech Republic (2.4%) and the United Kingdom (1.2%), while tourists from Austria had 6.0% fewer overnight stays.

istria county outperformed the rest of the country in june this year

In June 2026, Istria County once again recorded the highest number of overnight stays in the country, totalling 4.3 million, or 31.9% of all overnight stays in Croatia. Despite being the county with the most tourist overnight stays, overnight stays in Istria County fell by 10.0% compared to June 2025. Domestic tourists in Istria County recorded 219 thousand overnight stays (15.9% more than in June 2025), while foreign tourists recorded 4.1 million overnight stays (down 11.1% from the previous year’s June).

After Istria County came Split-Dalmatia County with 2.7 million overnight stays (20.0% of the Croatian total) and Primorje-Gorski Kotar County with 2.2 million (16.4%). Compared to June 2025, overnight stays were down 7.5% in Primorje-Gorski Kotar County and 1.7% in Split-Dalmatia County.

In June 2026, the highest number of overnight stays was recorded by tourists in two age groups: those under 14 years of age and those between 55 and 64 years of age. Each of these groups recorded 2.2 million overnight stays, accounting for 16.2% of the total.

World.title: More and More Filipinos Are Working in Croatia
World.content:
August the 12th, 2026 – More and more Filipinos are being registered as living and working in Croatia, with the vast majority employed in the tourism and trade sectors.

As Jadranka Dozan/Poslovni reports, over the first seven months of this year, a total of 106,400 permits were issued to citizens of third countries (countries outside of the EEA), of which almost two-thirds were for work in tourism and construction.

The number of issued work permits is reportedly falling, but Interior Ministry data doesn’t show the real number of workers from abroad. The latest data from the Ministry of the Interior on permits issued to foreign workers from so-called third countries only confirmed the continuation of the year-on-year decline in their overall number. This is partly a consequence of the fact that since March last year the maximum duration of permits has been extended from one to three years.

this “decline” isn’t straightforward

How much of this alleged decline is explained by that change in legal rules, and how much is contributed by generally tightened rules or some other reasons (such as meeting part of the need for workers through increased work engagement of domestic pensioners or, for example, returnees to Croatia), the Interior Ministry statistics don’t reveal.

In the first seven months of 2026, a total of 106,400 residence and work permits were issued to citizens of “third countries”, which is 7.5 percent less than last year. Looking only at July, almost 23 percent fewer were issued than last year.

seasonal employment

So far in 2026, the share of permits for seasonal jobs increased significantly, they’re actually up by 40 percent compared to last year – while those for new employment are down 31 percent, and permit extensions are up around 10 percent. Looking only at the month of July, Interior Ministry data reveals that a total of 12,282 positive decisions were issued for imported labour (compared to 15,905 in the same month last year). Almost every fourth of these, or more than 3,000 permits, was given for seasonal work, while just over 9,000 relate to new employment (just under 4,500) and permit extensions (just under 4,800).

40 percent is how much the number of permits for seasonal jobs has risen this year compared to last year, and it’s far from insignificant. Looking at the situation by activity, almost two-thirds of permits go to the two sectors where the import of workers is normally the most massive, tourism and hospitality, as well as construction. This applies both to those issued last month and to the total number issued since the beginning of the year. However, in construction there are 17 percent fewer this year than in the first seven months of last year, while in tourism and hospitality activities there are 5.4 percent more.

Of the other three most represented sectors when it comes to importing workers, an increase in the number of issued permits in 2026 is recorded only in trade. This also contributes to changes in the structure of issued permits in terms of the origin of workers. By far the largest growth is recorded for those issued to Filipinos – almost 50 percent higher than last year. Filipino workers, in addition to the tourism sector, are most often engaged by employers from the trade sector.

misleading statistics

The Interior Ministry’s records of work permits, however, fail to reveal many things and are certainly not the best indicator of the real situation regarding how many workers from third countries there are in Croatia. Experts on migration and demography have been pointing out the problem of recording foreign workers in general for a long time.

On the occasion of the recent publication of data by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics on migration for 2025, one of the more active among them, Tado Jurić, once again warned about the methodological challenges in this area. From the official data of the Interior Ministry and the CBS (according to which 56,700 immigrated foreign citizens were recorded last year), no one can say with certainty how many of them are actually in Croatia because these are records of different phenomena, he says.

For that reason, the number of insured persons in the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute (HZMO) is usually considered a somewhat more authoritative indicator. In its records in the middle of this year there were a little under 151,000 insured persons who are citizens of third countries (more precisely, with travel documents of those countries), which is about 29,000 more than at the end of last year. Although these are insured persons (which does not automatically mean employees), this is still roughly the indicator closest to reality, and it roughly implies that every 12th person who works and/or pays contributions in Croatia is a foreigner.

“practically half of croatia’s foreign workforce comes from africa and asia”

Given that practically half of the foreign workforce in Croatia today comes from Asia and Africa, migration experts have long emphasised that this requires active management of the processes, both in the context of integration and policies aimed at stronger activation of one’s own potentials. Due to low labour productivity in the public sector, it is often pointed out that there are certain employment reserves there for the entrepreneurial sector, but reforms of that kind do not come easily.

World.title: Almost All Istrian Beaches Have Excellent Quality Seawater
World.content:
August the 12th, 2026 – Almost all Istrian beaches have excellent quality seawater according to the latest measurements, with only four lagging behind.

The sea at Istrian beaches continues to be of exceptionally high quality. In the sixth examination of this year, conducted from the 28th of July to the 6th of August, as many as 98.2 percent of the seawater samples received an excellent rating. Index reports that the sea was sampled at a total of 222 measuring points on beaches from Savudrija to Brestova.

During the process of seawater sampling, the sea temperature ranged between 24 and 29 degrees, while the air temperature was from 24 to 33 degrees.

only four locations were less than exceptional

Excellent swimming seawater quality was recorded at 218 measuring points. Good quality was also recorded at one location, in Ližnjan at Matićev Pisk below the hotel. At three locations, the sea received a satisfactory rating only. These are AC Kažela – FKK in Medulin, Tarska vala in the Tar-Vabriga area, and the location near Hotel Molindrio in Poreč.

bacteria measuring

When examining the seawater, the quantities of intestinal enterococci and the bacterium Escherichia coli are determined as indicators of microbiological pollution. During the sampling process, meteorological conditions, sea temperature and salinity, as well as any visible pollution, are also recorded.

Based on the results of individual samples, the sea is classified as excellent, good or satisfactory. The results of all individual examinations are available via the online application of the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition.

World.title: PM: Land joining Madise in race 'should make the election interesting'
World.content:
Ülle Madise is now backed by more than 60 MPs, but Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) still believes TalTech rector Tiit Land will also enter Estonia's presidential race.

Michal said he supports Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise and believes she would make a good president.

"We have one candidate with the support of about 60 MPs, and more signatures are gradually coming in," Michal said Thursday, calling it good news. "This means the presidential election has its first candidate eligible to be elected in the Riigikogu."

The prime minister said said parties are still in talks with Land, the rector of Tallinn University of Technology, and Mart Helme, the founder and deputy chair of the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE), but expects Land to be nominated.

"That should make the election rounds in the Riigikogu interesting," he added.

'I don't understand what's stopping them'

Minister of Education and Research and Eesti 200 chair Kristina Kallas said the political expectations surrounding the election do not reflect the constitutional system established for electing the president.

"The idea that Estonia's president is simply appointed or that this is a contest between top officials makes a mockery of our constitutional order," Kallas said, emphasizing that the president's role in Estonia as head of state isn't significant enough to require such a broad public mandate.

"The law provides for the president to be elected by the Riigikogu," she added. "We don't have nationwide campaigns, debates or public forums."

Kallas praised the work the Riigikogu has put into the process over the summer, noting that the process is less a traditional election and moreso an agreement on who will represent Estonia for the next five years.

Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) and Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200). Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

With more than 60 MPs agreeing by now that that should be Madise, Kallas urged other parties to skip any political games, show good statesmanship and join in her support.

"If the other parties say they have no reservations or fundamental ideological objections to Madise, I don't understand what's stopping them from supporting her," the Eesti 200 chair said. "Our job is to come together and elect a president."

She added that Madise's international standing and strong knowledge of the Constitution would make her well suited to the role.

'This isn't some game'

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said every MP in his party's parliamentary group has already signed in support of Madise. "Eesti 200 stands 100 behind what we've said," he said.

He urged parties to put aside political maneuvering connected to the 2027 Riigikogu elections and focus first on their responsibility to Estonia.

"This isn't some domestic political game where it's all fun and games and we take shots at one another," Tsahnka continued. "Look around you — we haven't seen geopolitical turmoil like this since the Soviet Union, and it affects our security as well. Never forget that independence cannot be taken for granted."

The Riigikogu will convene to elect the next president of Estonia on September 2, with candidates to be formally nominated August 21–24.

World.title: AirBaltic says it will continue flying from Tallinn
World.content:
The future of Latvian airline airBaltic is in the hands of its creditors, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said. Potential strategic investors are waiting for airBaltic to become viable and profitable. Under the new business plan approved on Wednesday, the airline will fly to fewer destinations but with higher frequency.

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs stepped out for the first time from behind the wall of business‑secrecy surrounding airBaltic and admitted that the situation is very serious. According to Kulbergs, the state as the majority owner effectively lost control of the airline years ago, when €380 million worth of bonds were issued at an enormous 14.5 percent interest rate.

"No company can bear such a burden if no changes are made and no strategic plan is reviewed. They simply continued flying. The state is essentially no longer the owner — airBaltic is in the hands of lenders. Rights over the company were lost in 2024 when €380 million in bonds were issued," Kulbergs said.

Andris Kulbergs. Source: ERR

Now €225 million in bridge financing must be raised, using the bond collateral. The first bondholder meeting failed due to lack of quorum, and both the transport minister and airBaltic's leadership are now negotiating to ensure that the second meeting, planned for Monday, produces a result.

"The coming weeks are decisive. We will see whether bondholders support the chosen path and secure temporary financing, and whether the new business plan can attract new capital," Kulbergs said.

AirBaltic supervisory board vice‑chair Jurgis Sedlenieks confirmed to ERR that under the new business plan, the airline's main base will remain in Riga, and flights will continue from Tallinn and Vilnius. The number of aircraft will decrease and is expected to settle at around 40 in the future.

"The airline will reduce destinations, but flights to those that remain will operate several times a week. Some routes launched this summer from Tallinn — for example Tallinn–Vienna — will continue into winter. This shows that we are continuing in Estonia, which is a very important market for the company," Sedlenieks said.

According to the Latvian prime minister, strategic investors interested in airBaltic do exist, but they will not make a decision before the company's restructuring is complete.

"They are willing to continue negotiations once the company's strategy and issues related to lenders have been resolved," Kulbergs said.

The state cannot be the only party covering airBaltic's financial risks, even though it is one of Latvia's most important companies, the prime minister noted.

World.title: Wildlife expert: Rising bear numbers could increase risk of human attacks
World.content:
Estonia's bear population has grown for two decades, and one wildlife expert warns that new, tighter hunting limits could increase the risk of conflicts with people.

Recent court decisions have significantly restricted bear hunting in Estonia, and Peep Männil, a wildlife expert at the Environment Agency, expects the country's brown bear population to grow faster as a result.

That could mean more agricultural damage, greater impacts on other wildlife and more encounters with people, including potential attacks.

Estonia was home to about 1,100 brown bears as of fall 2025, according to agency estimates. The population has grown by an average of 5 percent a year over the past decade, with growth accelerating in recent years.

Männil explained that officials estimate bear numbers using sightings, particularly of females with cubs, rather than trying to count individual animals. More than 7,000 observations were recorded across Estonia last year, most by hunters and other wildlife enthusiasts using trail cameras.

The Environment Agency then maps and analyzes the resulting data, in the same approach used to estimate wolf, lynx and other wildlife populations.

No deadly attacks

While the abundance of sightings and trail-camera images can make it seem like there are suddenly far more bears in Estonia, Männil said bear numbers have actually been growing steadily for about 20 years already.

"The growth rate of the bear population will likely increase now, which is logical," he said, commenting on recently tightened hunting restrictions.

The expert said a growing bear population could lead to more crop damage as well as affect moose numbers, as bears prey heavily on moose calves in their first weeks of life.

"Studies in Sweden have found that the impact [on moose] can be quite significant," he added.

While the risk to people remains relatively low in Estonia, Männil warned that a larger bear population still also means a greater chance of dangerous encounters.

Seven bear attacks on people have been recorded in Estonia in the past 25 years. None were fatal, but three resulted in injuries, most recently in 2022. Four occurred during hunting situations, after the bear had been shot.

"That number is too small to draw any conclusions about an upward trend, but the likelihood of more such incidents will certainly increase," he said.

Simple safety tips

Männil explained that attacks here are generally defensive rather than predatory, and can occur when a person and bear unexpectedly encounter each other at close range. The possibility of an encounter, however, should not keep people out of the woods.

"It would be so unfortunate if people stopped foraging for mushrooms or spending time in nature because they're afraid there are too many bears," he said.

With risks rising as bear numbers grow, the agency expert stressed that careful wildlife management is increasingly important.

"One of the broader goals of hunting is to prevent these kinds of large swings in wildlife populations as much as possible," Männil said. "They're no good for the species themselves or for the balance between species."

While urban sightings do happen, encounters are more likely while hiking or foraging. A few simple tips shared by the Estonian Hunters' Society (EJS) can help keep you safe if you run into a brown bear in the wild.

World.title: Argo Ideon: The purpose of Russia's 'parliamentary elections' is to secure Kremlin power
World.content:
The parties participating in the political performance are cogs in a totalitarian system; real opposition in Russia has either been physically eliminated or driven into exile abroad, writes Argo Ideon.

With Russia's Duma "elections" scheduled for September 18–20, a little more than a month remains. Work is underway to ensure the numbers look presentable for the Kremlin. Vladimir Putin is conducting a propaganda tour in the country's east — an area out of reach of Ukrainian drone strikes — visiting Novosibirsk and even the Kuril Islands, which Russia seized from Japan. Meanwhile, courts are busy cleansing the ballot lists of opponents.

Many observers predict that after the elections, Russia will face a broad mobilization for the war in Ukraine — either fully public or somewhat concealed to reduce tension. Unfortunately, that is a more consequential event than any election result.

It is clear that Russia has long ceased to hold parliamentary elections in the Western democratic sense. Over the first quarter of this century, even the few remaining features resembling real elections have largely disappeared.

What remains is a political staging whose purpose is to fill the State Duma building in Moscow with loyal puppets competing to praise Vladimir Putin's imperial worldview. They also continue the conveyor belt of repressive laws that has characterized the current Duma.

Governance in Russia typically runs vertically. This means that a lower‑level boss — such as a mayor or regional governor — must ensure that goals set by the presidential administration are met: what voter turnout must be, how many votes certain parties must receive. And the votes appear. Those who fail are deemed ineffective leaders. Lower levels then bend over backwards to make sure everything proceeds as prescribed.

"What remains is a political staging whose purpose is to fill the State Duma building in Moscow with loyal puppets."

Since access to the elections is strictly limited from the candidacy stage onward, the disciplined voting process adds little from Moscow's perspective. But the system must still function, the gears must keep turning. Otherwise, spontaneous developments and "anarchy" might occur, and people could get the idea that anyone might be allowed to come to power.

The parties currently in the State Duma are cogs in this machinery — "cartel parties," to use Estonian political veteran Mart Helme's expression. If a voter for some reason does not want to vote for a United Russia candidate, they can choose the slightly more social‑branded A Just Russia, the Communist Party appealing to Soviet nostalgia, New People emphasizing small‑business interests, and others.

But when it is necessary to support the Kremlin on key issues — such as annexing a neighboring country's territory or killing Ukrainian civilians — these pocket parties all sing in the same choir, some more eagerly than others.

The fiercest competition in the Duma is among those who demand more effective destruction of Russia's enemies and settling scores with the opposing side. In the past, the radical‑patriotic role was mainly filled by the Liberal Democratic Party led by Vladimir Zhirinovsky. Now, with Vladimir Volfovich gone for several years, the LDPR is losing its accustomed niche.

All Russian party leaders beat the same drum, starting with United Russia chairman Dmitry Medvedev. His social media posts insulting Europe and the entire Western world have become a phenomenon of their own. In the early 2000s, Medvedev was still seen as representing the more liberal wing of the Russian elite, with a fondness for 1970s rock stars like Deep Purple and Black Sabbath…

Real opposition in Russia has been physically destroyed or driven abroad. Boris Nemtsov and Alexey Navalny — who were able to mobilize voters — have been killed. Much of the political emigration deemed "offenders" by the Russian state has been subjected to "civil death" under rules established by the Duma — they cannot use property in Russia or most state services.

Recently, the only party openly calling for peace in Ukraine, Yabloko, was banned from participating in the elections. But even among Russian émigrés, opinions differ on Yabloko's role.

One of Russia's best‑known dissidents, Vladimir Kara‑Murza, writes in The Washington Post that Yabloko became a channel through which Russian citizens could legally express opposition to the war in Ukraine, and the Kremlin grew afraid of them. "Putin panicked," Kara‑Murza argues.

Russian publicist Igor Eidman, living in Germany, instead says the authorities did not start fearing Yabloko; rather, developments in Russia's state system have reached a point where even symbolic or marginal dissent has no place.

"There is no longer any polyphony: all actors must speak with one voice, the same voice," Eidman writes on social media. "The state is returning to classic Stalinist‑type totalitarianism."

World.title: Paide out of UEFA Conference League after Rapid Vienna loss
World.content:
Eesti Meistriliiga side Paide Linnameeskond are out of the UEFA Conference League after losing their third-round qualifier second leg 2-0 away to Austrian legends Rapid Vienna.

Paide's route to the third-round qualifier saw them beat Lithuanian club Hegelmann 4-1 on aggregate, before overcoming Azerbaijani side Zira 2-1, also on aggregate.

However, a 4-1 defeat at home in the first leg last week had left Paide's chances almost hopeless, and they were unable to pull off a miracle on the road, exiting 6-1 on aggregate.

On Wednesday, Rapid forward Marco Tilio opened the scoring in the 37th minute, while Louis Schaub converted a penalty in the 82nd.

The 32-time Austrian Bundesliga winners enjoyed 65 percent of possession and saw as many as 23 shots, seven of them on target, compared with the visitors' two and one.

Rapid Vienna next face arguably an even bigger club, Portugal's Benfica, who similarly dispatched Scottish Premier League side Heart of Midlothian 6-1 on aggregate in their third-round qualifier.

World.title: Eesti Pank to issue Hiiumaa‑themed €2 coin
World.content:
The central motif of the coin is Hiiumaa's landmark, the Kõpu Lighthouse, surrounded by sea waves, with the light beams reflecting the striped pattern of Hiiumaa's traditional folk skirt. This pattern is an important part of the island's identity, symbolizing continuity and resilience, and representing the security of the home island.

The design is by Kaupo Kangro.

The Kõpu Lighthouse was completed in its original form in 1531 and is the third‑oldest operating lighthouse in the world.

One million coins dedicated to Hiiumaa will be minted and released into circulation through retail channels. The coin will be valid as official legal tender throughout the euro area.

Hiiumaa, known for its distinctive nature and long maritime history, will open Eesti Pank's new coin series dedicated to Estonia's counties. The aim of the series is to highlight the diversity and cultural uniqueness of Estonia's regions.

World.title: Economy minister rejects proposed restrictions on nicotine products
World.content:
Economy Minister Erkki Keldo declined to approve a draft bill aimed at curbing the use of nicotine products among young people as the proposed changes could have a significant impact on sellers and importers.

The restrictions proposed by the Ministry of Social Affairs and the Ministry of Justice would allow nicotine pouches, nicotine strips and nicotine sprays containing no more than four milligrams of nicotine per gram to be sold in Estonia. The aim is to reduce the use of nicotine products among young people.

Erkki Keldo sent a letter to the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs on Wednesday informing it that he had declined to approve the draft bill. Keldo said the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications supports protecting the health of children and young people and curbing the illegal sale of nicotine products, but considers it important that measures restricting freedom of enterprise be sufficiently justified and proportionate.

Snus. Source: Flickr

"The changes proposed in the draft bill could significantly affect manufacturers, importers, wholesalers and retailers of nicotine products operating in Estonia. The explanatory memorandum does not adequately assess the extent of these impacts or provide a convincing justification for the proposed maximum nicotine content of 4 mg/g for nicotine-containing products related to tobacco products," Keldo said.

He noted that the draft bill's maximum nicotine content of four milligrams per gram is based on Latvia's approach, but said this was not sufficient justification for restricting freedom of enterprise.

"The explanatory memorandum does not indicate the nicotine content of nicotine pouches and other products covered by the bill currently on the Estonian market, what proportion of products currently marketed legally would comply with the proposed limit or how many businesses and products would be affected by the change," the economy minister said.

He is also dissatisfied that the draft bill does not include a comparative analysis of approaches taken by other EU member states or explain why Latvia's regulations are the best model for Estonia.

Keldo said the explanatory memorandum needs to be supplemented with a comparison of different options. The impact of the limit on the health of children and young people, the risk of accidental poisoning, businesses, the functioning of the legal market and consumer behavior should also be analyzed.

The data presented in the explanatory memorandum concern products containing e-cigarette liquid, but does not address the impact of the changes on nicotine pouches, strips, sprays and heated nicotine sticks.

"We ask that the impact assessment be expanded to separately cover all product categories regulated by the draft bill and the requirements proposed for them," the minister said.

Keldo also wants the impact of the changes on Estonian manufacturers, exports, employment and regional businesses to be examined, along with their impact on the legal market, illegal trade and tax revenue.

"Possible substitution behavior must also be analyzed, including whether some consumers could switch to products with unregulated contents or to other tobacco and nicotine products and what impact this could have on achieving the draft bill's public health objective," Keldo said.

The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications is also dissatisfied with a provision in the draft bill stipulating that products may not contain substances that produce a flavor or aroma other than tobacco or menthol and that only substances listed in a specific regulation may be used to provide those flavors. However, the explanatory memorandum does not explain why those particular substances are considered suitable or what costs businesses could incur in reformulating existing products.

Keldo said the bill's relationship with the planned update of the European Union's legal framework for tobacco and nicotine products should also be assessed.

The Ministry of Social Affairs has previously said that people are starting to use nicotine products at increasingly younger ages. While young people previously tried nicotine at ages 15 or 16, they are now doing so at around age 11. Nicotine pouches and e-cigarettes are the most common products used by those starting out.

Estonia's so-called Superministry building housing several government ministries. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Just over one-fifth of the nicotine products currently on the market comply with the requirements proposed in the draft bill. Around 60 percent of products would have to be reformulated, while nearly one-fifth would have to be removed from the market.

Several European countries have tightened restrictions on nicotine products in recent years. Latvia raised the minimum age for purchasing tobacco and nicotine products to 20 two years ago. No such proposal is currently under consideration in Estonia.

The new rules are planned to take effect in 2028, although the exact date will be determined as the draft bill moves through the legislative process.
