Tech.title: Equifax Customers Can Claim Part of a $2.2M Class Action Settlement This Month
Tech.content:
Users of Equifax’s consumer credit reports service may be eligible to claim part of an upcoming $2.2 million settlement payout. The case centered on allegations that Equifax violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act, a federal statute that dictates credit reporting companies must “follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.”

The class action lawsuit, Bradberry v. Equifax Information Services LLC, alleged that in 2022, Equifax “wrongfully reported duplicates of negative accounts” on certain consumer reports, and that these duplicated debt tradelines are a result of the company having inadequate datakeeping policies and procedures. The lawsuit alleges that Equifax “negligently and recklessly disseminated false and damaging information” regarding the credit of certain customers.

Essentially, the lawsuit alleges that Equifax’s negligent reporting made some customers’ debts appear larger than they actually were, potentially creating situations where affected individuals couldn’t secure loans, credit cards, mortgages and other lines of credit.

The plaintiff, Charmayne Bradberry, filed the suit in the US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia. Bradberry said that she received a report showing the same $305 collection account twice, and that each instance showed separate “opened” and “reported” dates for the debt. She alleges that her credit score dropped severely following this report, which may have prevented her from securing a vital mortgage application.

Bradberry is one of 37,651 customers Equifax identified as having received reports with duplicate debt tradelines.

Equifax has denied any wrongdoing and denied that settlement class members were harmed by its actions, and the court has not ruled in favor of either side. The settlement was agreed upon by both parties, and the court has preliminarily approved the $2.2 million payment, subject to a final approval hearing.

The settlement website is live now. The hearing is scheduled to take place on Oct. 6, during which the court will confirm the settlement sum, allocate funds for attorneys’ fees and create a plan to distribute money to the affected class members.

While some class action lawsuits automatically pay out from the agreed-upon sum, that isn’t the case with Bradberry v. Equifax. Affected individuals need to file a claim and provide valid payment information by Sept. 1 to receive a share of the funds.

If you wish to opt out of or object to the settlement, you must do so by the same Sept. 1 deadline. Failure to do so will mean you remain part of the settlement class and forfeit your right to separately sue Equifax for this incident.

Who can be part of the Equifax settlement?

Not every Equifax customer is automatically eligible to claim part of the settlement. The money is reserved for people who received reports with duplicated collection account information that reflected larger sums of debt than existed in reality.

In order to join, you must meet the following qualifications:

Be a living individual in the US or its territories. Received one of the identified Duplicate Reporting Letters from Equifax between August and September 2022.

The settlement class in this case is extremely well-defined. Equifax identified 37,651 people who received duplicated reports. These individuals are the qualifying settlement class members.

Affected class members need to file a paper claim or log in through the settlement website in order to receive a payout. In order to file a claim online, you need to use the unique settlement member ID number included within the initial communication sent to affected individuals. This communication was sent out via postcard and email.

How much will the Equifax settlement pay out?

The total payment for each claimant is capped at $600, but actual payouts will depend on how many settlement class members file claims and how much money the court sets aside for attorney and administrative fees.

Whether or not settlement class members file a claim, they will receive six months of Equifax Complete credit monitoring services, including credit reports, credit score monitoring and up to $500,000 insurance for identity theft-related expenses.

During the claims process, class members must select a valid payment method for their share of the settlement funds. According to the paper claim form, you can choose to have the money sent to a PayPal, Venmo or Zelle account, a virtual prepaid card or a check.

If you’re eligible to claim a piece of the settlement sum, you must file by Sept. 1. Payments will be distributed after the court’s final approval hearing, assuming there are no appeals.

Tech.title: This $35 Coffee Maker Fits in My Pocket and Comes on All My Camping Trips
Tech.content:
Miir’s Pourigami sets a new standard for portable, pour-over coffee. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Brewing coffee while camping presents a unique set of challenges. On more occasions than I care to admit, I’ve spilled a freshly made coffee thanks to an unsteady camping table or stone underfoot. But a rigorous day of outdoor adventuring calls for caffeine — full stop. As a professional coffee writer, I demand something more elevated than packets of instant crystals.

Having used several portable brewers, I finally landed on one that ticks the most boxes: The MiiR Pourigami. Once assembled, the pyramid-shaped drip brewer fits atop any travel mug. Taken apart, it’s slim enough to fit into my pants pocket. It functions like standard pour-overs, meaning I can dial in tasting notes to my liking. The laughably simple yet nifty setup lets you play barista in any environment.

Miir Pourigami Coffee Maker $35 at Amazon

The Miir Pourigami brewer in a nutshell

Yup, that’s a coffee maker in my hand. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Right out of the box, the Pourigami looks sleek. Disassembled, the brewer consists of three thin stainless-steel trapezoids. I can’t imagine the pieces bending or chipping — that’s crucial, as I’m prone to breaking camping equipment. It folds up flat for storage, smaller than 10 by 16 centimeters. Weighing just shy of 8 ounces, the brewer isn’t featherweight, but it offers great portability nevertheless. Contained in an unassuming synthetic case, the Pourigami seamlessly fits into any bag.

I’m terrible at paper origami, but assembling this brewer into the pyramidal shape is a breeze. It only takes me about 20 seconds to slip the three indents into their slots. The completed dripper holds steady without a wobble and comes apart just as easily.

Essential Camping Tech, All Chosen by CNET Editors See at Cnet

Put together, the interior forms a pyramid shape that can accommodate any No. 2 cone-shaped filters. I find that Miir’s own filters, available for purchase online function most reliably, creating steady streams without slipping. The brand’s paper-based filters are compostable, which is a small but satisfying environmental win, but compatible filters are easy to find. Either way, the Miir Pourigami is simple to set up and get to brewing.

Brewing with the Pourigami

The Pourigami functions much like other pour-over coffee devices.

If you’ve used pour-over vessels such as a V60, Chemex or a Kalita Wave, the Miir Pourigami is familiar territory. The dripper requires a hot water source, the aforementioned paper filter, and a cup or carafe to catch the coffee. A kitchen scale and thermometer help brew with utmost accuracy, but I’ve produced solid cups while eyeballing proportions outdoors.

It’s best to follow a brewing ratio to extract the most out of the brewer, especially when familiarizing yourself with its flow. The Miir brand suggests 21 grams for single-origin beans and 23 grams for blends, each extracted with 300 milliliters of water. Using water heated to 90 degrees Celsius, I’ve found these proportions reliable, as long as extraction is completed by the 3.5-minute mark.

The Pourigami functions similarly to a Chemex but with better portability. Taylor Martin/CNET

Compared to my V60, the Miir Pourigami takes longer to drain, so a coarser grind helps keep water moving. As a result, the vessel is best suited for full-bodied cups of medium- and dark-roasted coffees. The grind quality is crucial: You’ll want a coarse yet uniform consistency. I’ve used both the portable MiiR Coffee Hand Grinder and the Baratza Encore to great success; I would avoid using a blade grinder for this setup, though. While I’m away from home, I’ve asked coffee shops to grind beans — I request a consistency one click coarser than a V60. Preground coffee is the most convenient way to brew on the move.

The Pourigami’s steep interior makes saturating coffee grounds easy — no need to carry a gooseneck kettle alongside. I’ve used jet-boil-powered camping kettles and even cooking pots to make excellent cups of coffee, making sure to use hot water that’s off the boil. As long as I’m timing the process, using the Miir Pourigami is undemanding.

What does Pourigami filter coffee taste like?

The coffee I brew turns out light-bodied, but rarely weak or watery. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

As with all pour-over coffee, the beans strongly influence the flavor. I’ve produced the best-tasting MiiR Pourigami cups using medium-roast blends — think grocery-store beans like Stumptown’s Holler Mountain Blend. Such bags respond well to the requisite coarser grind and are forgiving in outdoor scenarios. The Miir Pourigami translates gentle notes of acidity and sweetness, seldom leaning into burnt flavors. The coffee turns out light-bodied, similar to other filter setups, but I’ve never brewed a cup that tastes weak or watery.

If there’s one downside to this dripper, it’s that the coffee occasionally turns out too acidic, a sign of under-extraction. For this reason, I avoid brewing delicate light roasts with the Pourigami — not that I’m packing fancy beans for camping anyway. A bold, balanced medium roast cup hits the spot after a night in a tent.

Is the Pourigami worth it?

Coffee makers don’t get much simpler and more portable than the Pourigami. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

At home, I’m not often assembling my Pourgami, instead settling on the trusty espresso machine or extracting delicate cups of V60. When I’m brewing outside of the house, though, the Pourigami is my top choice. In addition to camping, I’ll pack the brewer away in my suitcase for air travel, making the occasional cup on the go.

Before acquiring a model, I used to camp with a bulky plastic V60 dripper, which I inevitably fractured by cramming it in with the rest of my camping equipment. The AeroPress is sturdier, but it can be difficult to find a surface suitable for firm plunging. Compact and durable, the Miir Pourigami wins on logistical ease, making it easy to incorporate into a car-camping, backpacking or even a bike-packing setup.

Sold for $35, it’s a thoughtfully designed coffee gadget that justifies the price. The inventive design isn’t a trade-off for coffee quality and I’m happy to use the Pourigami several days in a row — the steel material is a breeze to clean. Whether I’m at home or on the move, the brewer doesn’t occupy much space, making it a reliable favorite.

Tech.title: Rivian R1S, R1T See 2027 Updates, Including Second-Row Captain’s Chairs
Tech.content:
American electric vehicle manufacturer Rivian is rolling out 2027 model year updates to the R1S SUV and R1T pickup this week. Alongside a revised trim-level naming scheme that brings the R1 models in line with the newer R2, Rivian’s R1S can now be had with a new second-row captain’s chair configuration that trades a bit of seat capacity for improved comfort and convenience. Meanwhile, the R1T electric truck gets a new all-season wheel-and-tire option, rebalancing on-road range with off-road capability.

Upgraded seating

The biggest material update affects the full-size R1S, which is now available with a six-seat configuration that swaps the SUV’s second-row bench for captain’s chairs. The new buckets get individual armrests that fold flush when not in use and a push-to-release cupholder that accommodates large water bottles, while retaining the bench’s heated surfaces and car-seat tie-downs. The fold-flat design makes way for bulky cargo, but the unobstructed center pass-through allows long, narrow gear like surfboards or skis to stretch through from the rear without having to fold the seats down or give up its six-passenger capacity.

Pricing for the new seat setup ranges from $1,500 to $4,500, depending on the trim level and required and optional equipment.

Rivian says the new second-row configuration is its “most requested interior feature since launch” among R1S shoppers. Brandon De La Cruz / Rivian

Renamed trim levels

Other changes bring Rivian’s flagship trim naming scheme into alignment with the R2. The automaker is largely retiring the Dual, Tri and Quad motor-count naming for most trims. The dual-motor models are now called Premium, offering the same 533 horsepower, 610 pound-feet of torque, and up to 329 miles of range as before. Premium buyers can spec an optional power upgrade that bumps output to 665 hp and 829 lb-ft or upgrade to a bigger battery that stretches the cruising range to 410 miles on the R1S or 420 miles on the R1T.

Performance is the new moniker for the 850-hp tri-motor layout, with 1,103 lb-ft of torque and 371 miles of range. Finally, at the top of the line, the 374-mile Quad trim’s name goes unchanged. It’s still good for 1,025 hp and 1,198 lb-ft, hitting 0 to 60 mph in 2.5 seconds and the quarter-mile in 10.5 seconds in its Launch Mode — a claim I previously verified on a prepped drag strip.

The interior color and material themes for the R1 models have also been renamed to match R2. Premium models are available with Black Mountain (black) or Ocean Coast (gray) upholstery, while Performance and Quad buyers can choose from Slate Sky (gray with walnut wood), Black Mountain Signature (black with ash wood accents) and Ocean Coast Signature (gray with weathered driftwood).

R1T and R1S are now also available in the Silver Esker paint option, a liquid-metal finish first introduced on R2, which replaces LA Silver as the standard no-cost paint option for the 2027 model year.

The larger Rivian R1 models inherit the new Silver Esker paint color from their younger sibling, the R2. Brandon De La Cruz / Rivian

Adventure wheel and tires

R1T gains a new “Adventure” 20-inch all-season wheel-and-tire package as standard equipment on the Premium trim level, trading some on-road range for added off-road traction and grip when compared to some of the larger, lower-friction options available. This combo is also available as a no-cost option on the R1T Performance. That is, unless you count the cost to EPA-estimated range, which drops to 300 miles on the R1T Premium, 380 miles on the Premium Long Range, and 348 miles on the Performance with the new rolling stock.

The 2027 model-year Rivian R1T and R1S are now available to configure on Rivian’s website and in showrooms. R1S starts at $83,990, and R1T starts at $79,990, pricing that is also unchanged from the 2026 model year.

Tech.title: Ninja Just Launched Its First Water Filter. Here’s What It Does That Others Don’t
Tech.content:
Water filtration is a booming category, and at-home units come in a range of formats: under-sink attachments, whole-house systems, water filter pitchers and countertop dispensers.

Ever the innovator, Ninja has jumped into the category with the launch of HydraSense, a slim countertop water filter that removes more than 80 contaminants (including forever chemicals, lead, microplastics and pharmaceuticals) and does a few things its competitors don’t.

The Best Countertop Water Filters, Lab-Tested by CNET See at CNET

I got a firsthand look at the HydraSense at Ninja’s New York headquarters, where the product team walked me through its unique features and also showed off the filter’s pure power by running a batch of Kool-Aid through it.

Here’s what it does.

Filters out the bad stuff but leaves the good

Red Kool-Aid run through the HydraSense came out crystal clear. David Watsky/CNET

Reverse osmosis filters are the best for pure filtering power. The knock is that they strip water of minerals, which can leave water tasting bland. HydraSense’s oversized and especially dense activated carbon filter preserves naturally occurring minerals, including calcium, magnesium and potassium, for better-tasting water.

I sipped some fresh from the spout, and it tasted as crisp and clean as any I’ve had from the many filters I’ve tested.

In a demo, the product team filtered a batch of freshly made red Kool-Aid through the HydraSense. What emerged was perfectly clear liquid that tasted like clean water with no residual fruit punch flavor.

Filters 80+ contaminants, with certifications to prove it

The HydraSense activated carbon filter [left] is bigger and denser than a standard Brita filter.

If you’re wondering how well the filter works, you don’t have to take Ninja’s word for it. The HydraSense is certified by the National Sanitation Foundation, the most rigorous water filter testing body, to remove chlorine, chloramine, lead, volatile organic compounds, PFAS (forever chemicals) and microplastics.

Loads of filters on the market claim to reduce or eliminate these contaminants via in-house or third-party testing, but regulatory certifications leave nothing in question.

Lets you know when the filter needs changing

Many filtration systems require you to guess when the filter needs changing, but not this model. David Watsky/CNET

The bulk of the water filters I’ve tested have no system to let you know when the filter needs changing. It becomes a guessing game, and keeping track of how much water you’ve put through the machine is pretty much impossible.

HydraSense has a built-in monitor that lets you know when the filter is nearing the end of its life so you don’t end up changing it too soon or not soon enough. A single filter is good for 120 gallons, and replacements cost $40.

Filters fast. Like, really fast

When testing countertop water filters for CNET, one downside for most of the machines was slow filtering time — sometimes as much as an hour or more to filter a gallon. The HydraSense uses a unique pressure system to push water through the filter so it dispenses immediately. The feature is especially handy for power hydrators and families that burn through drinking water fast.

I’m a fan of the Rorra gravity filter, but it takes far longer than Ninja’s to strip water of contaminants. David Watsky

While water comes out fast, there’s a handy slow pour setting so you can fill ice trays without making a mess. You can also set the machine to dispense water in pours of 6, 8, 10 and 12 ounces.

Adjustable pour settings allow you to start dispensing and walk away.

The price is right, too

At $200 — currently discounted to $160 for launch — the HydraSense represents one of the best-value water filters I’ve seen. Reverse osmosis systems like the AquaTru Carafe cost nearly twice as much. Gravity filters such as the Rorra and Boroux, which work well but slowly, typically start at around $300 and go up from there.

Ninja’s newly launched HydraSense has a slim build and features you won’t find on most water filters. David Watsky/CNET

It’s closest competitor is the $120 Brita Hub. It too is certified to filter roughly 80 contaminants and does so quickly using a similar pressure system. But there’s no filter life monitor or slow pour settings, and the plastic build is notably cheaper.

The HydraSense is available starting today on Ninja’s website.

Tech.title: YouTube TV and DirecTV Stream Users Could Be Owed Money From Disney. Here’s the Deadline
Tech.content:
A federal antitrust lawsuit filed in 2022 accused Disney of using its ownership of ESPN and other in-demand programming to require streaming services to include those channels in their base packages — a practice that, plaintiffs alleged, made it impossible for providers to offer cheaper, sports-free options and kept prices artificially high across the industry.

Disney settled the case for $50 million without admitting liability. The settlement covers YouTube TV and DirecTV Stream subscribers, including DirecTV Now and AT&T TV Now accounts, who had active subscriptions at any point between April 1, 2019 and March 31, 2026. Now, the deadline to file a claim is Sept. 8.

To be eligible for a payout, you had to have bought a subscription to either YouTube TV or DirecTV — or both — between April 1, 2019, and March 31, 2026. DirecTV subscriptions might have been called DirecTV Stream, DirecTV Now or AT&T TV Now.

How to apply for the settlement

If you’re part of the settlement, you will likely get a notice in your USPS mailbox or your email inbox. Check your junk or spam folders in case your email service filtered it. The deadline for claiming a payment is Sept. 8.

If you get a notice, go to this website and log in with the ID and PIN provided on the settlement notice. You will need to verify your YouTube TV or DirecTV Stream subscription.

If you don’t get a notice but believe you are eligible for the cash settlement, send an email to info@OnlineTVSettlement.com or print out a PDF version of the claim form and send it via snail mail to:

Biddle v. Disney

Settlement Administrator

P.O. Box 4720

Portland, OR 97208-4720

Printed settlement claims must be postmarked by Sept. 8.

The settlement terms specify that 90% of the money will go to payees in these states and territories: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Guam, Hawaii, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oregon, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, West Virginia and Wisconsin.

The remaining 10% will go to settlement members in other states.

Why the lawsuit?

In Biddle v. Disney, (PDF) filed in 2022, the plaintiffs alleged that Disney violated federal and state antitrust and consumer protection laws by forcing YouTube TV, DirecTV and FuboTV subscribers to pay more for livestreaming TV. The $50 million settlement does not apply to FuboTV plaintiffs, who have not yet settled with Disney.

The plaintiffs alleged that Disney forced streaming platforms to bundle content from expensive channels such as ESPN and Hulu — both owned by Disney — into base packages, thereby escalating the subscription prices for those packages. It was alleged that prices for YouTube TV base package subscriptions went up from $35 to $65.

“Since Disney acquired operational control over Hulu in May 2019, prices across the SLPTV [Streaming Live Pay Television] Market, including for YouTube TV and DirecTV Stream, have nearly doubled,” the lawsuit alleged.

Disney denies violating any laws. There will be a hearing on Jan. 14, 2027, for final approval of the settlement.

A representative for Disney did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: New Twitch Feature Uses Channel Content to Train AI Without Asking Permission
Tech.content:
On Wednesday, Twitch confirmed reports that the streaming channel was using channel content to train Amazon’s AI models. While we aren’t sure how long the training feature has been active, Twitch has now added an opt-out button to its settings that will allow creators to turn the feature off. However, it is automatically enabled unless its users take action.

AI models, like the ones Amazon uses for Alexa Plus and other projects, require large amounts of content to train them to piece together accurate language or images. The Twitch platform is overflowing with such content, featuring large amounts of video, audio spoken by creators and text in stream chats. However, people who haven’t consented to training may not want their voice, words or video to be analyzed by AI and used in future prompts.

Representatives from Amazon and Twitch did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Head to Twitch security settings to find this opt-out option. Twitch

Twitch’s latest FAQ states, “When you allow training, that means that your content may be used for future Gen AI model improvements. An example of what happens when you allow your content to be used for training a GenAI content model is that your audio might help refine models that create speech to text, which would help improve captions at Twitch but would also help improve captions across Amazon.”

To turn off this feature, you can head to Twitch account settings and toggle off the feature that says Training for Generative AI. Twitch says you can still use other AI-powered features like Automods and campaign optimization even if you opt out of training.

Questions persist on how this AI Twitch training works

Questions remain about how Twitch chats and other elements are affected. DisobeyArt/Getty

It’s unclear what this means for chat on a Twitch channel. You don’t have to be a content creator to participate in a stream, so it’s worth asking whether chats from a streamer’s fans are also being used for this training. Twitch makes no mention of chat or how it’s affected by the training feature, but there could be consent issues around analyzing audience members’ contributions as well as the stream itself.

Many Twitch users also stream other live content, including other creators’ channels. This creates a potential conflict when the original streamer opts out of AI training, but the streamer rebroadcasting their content has AI training enabled. In that case, the AI model could still gain access to the original streamer’s content without their direct consent.

Twitch has also faced legal challenges over copyrighted music in the past, while some content creators have used various methods to circumvent the platform’s music restrictions. Depending on how training data is collected, Amazon could also capture copyrighted music from streaming services for use in its AI models, potentially creating additional legal concerns.

Tech.title: My Favorite Things from Made by Google 2026
Tech.content:
Google showed off its new Pixel lineup at its Made By Google 2026 event on Wednesday in New York City, but it wasn’t a typical big-tech announcement that gave the public its first look at new devices — that happened in the morning.

Perhaps Google chose to show its Pixel products off hours ahead of its event because a lot of details were leaked in advance, possibly leading the company to avoid following the traditional 10 a.m. PT show. Official details of the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, Pixel 11 Pro Fold foldable, Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch and Pixel Tag tracker were released at 7 a.m. PT, letting people get good looks at all the devices before they were officially announced during the show, which started at 6 p.m. ET.

Be sure to check out all of CNET’s coverage, including hands-on experience and Andrew Lanxon’s exclusive photo walk through Paris with the Pixel 11 Pro XL. After you’ve loaded browser tabs with each of those, let’s move on to what stood out today.

Live human presenters who can think on their feet

Apple has switched to almost entirely prerecorded keynotes, and while Samsung’s Galaxy Unpacked had live presenters on stage in front of an audience, they mostly delivered rehearsed and teleprompted scripts as they debuted their new devices.

Google remembers that a product release is a show and brought hosts who can be entertaining.

Host Trevor Noah and Google Senior Vice President Rick Osterloh chat at the beginning of the Made By Google 2026 event. Screenshot by Tyler Graham/CNET

Last year, Jimmy Fallon bounded around a set that felt more like his Late Night studio than an auditorium. This year brings comedian (and former late-night talk show host) Trevor Noah as host, who also interviewed people from Google in a multi-camera talk show environment.

Although some of Google’s folks did have a measure of polished presenter training going on, they had to bounce off Noah’s impromptu interjections. At one point, he said, “I’m the one who’s supposed to make sure nothing goes wrong. I mean it’s live – I’ll make sure everything goes wrong.” There were some awkward moments, to be sure, but I spent the time always curious just how Noah would react.

Trevor Noah and Joël Yawili text Yawili’s mother in multiple languages. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

But a demonstration of the Rambler dictation feature with Google’s Joël Yawili, where Yawili got Noah to text his mother in English and French, was conversational and funny. Yawili surprised Noah by saying that he was also originally from Johannesburg, and at times, it looked as if they needed to remind themselves they were there to show features, not just banter among themselves.

Live demos

Live demonstrations of technology can be the third rail of product announcements — crucial to see, but sometimes disastrous if they fail in front of viewers. But Google included several live demos during the event of new features debuting on the Pixel 11 series. That led to some fun moments, such as when Noah used his finger to wiggle the screen when using the new Rambler technology saying, “Wait, so are you guys seeing the screen with me? I’m controlling. Oh damn, that’s me.”

Also great was the demonstration of American Sign Language-to-text, where Google director of product inclusion and equity Annie Jean-Baptiste had a conversation with deaf actor Daniel Durant, who communicated in ASL.

Magic Capture does even more of the picture-taking for you

Is pressing the shutter button in the Camera app too haaaarrd? Have you wished the camera in your smartphone could do even more of the work, not just come up with well-exposed photos in all sorts of lighting conditions? Well, you’re in luck, because Magic Capture will do it all.

I hope my sarcasm as a photographer came through there, because now I’m going to tell you about the reality of picture taking: We miss shots all the time. We realize later we could have framed them better and crop them so everyone things we nailed it on the first try. We sometimes aren’t as quick with the shutter press to grab the shot we really wanted.

That’s a big part of why photography is appealing: it’s work, it takes practice and making a quality photo is a great feeling.

But most people just want to point their phone at a subject and snap a good picture. Magic Capture is another tool to help them do that without stressing over capturing the perfect moment. You point the camera at a scene, and the feature grabs shots for you, no shutter button-mashing required.

JuJu Watkins, Kenn Sulaimon and Jesser look at a photo shot using the Pixel 11 Pro’s Magic Capture feature. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Smartphone cameras are already making dozens of micro-captures for every shutter press, so Magic Capture is a logical extension of that process. It records video and then pulls out the best frames as still photos. At the event, it was demonstrated by Google’s Kenny Sulaimon live from Brooklyn Bridge Park with YouTuber Jesser and college basketball star JuJu Watkins shooting hoops and capturing stills of the action.

I’m reserving my full opinion about Magic Capture until I’ve had a chance to try it out – is it really making smart decisions about what to capture? – but for now, I’m going to embrace Magic Capture as a way to help non-photographers make better photos.

Pixel Tag, you’re it

The Apple AirTag has been a quiet giant success for years, but AirTags don’t work as well with Android phones as they do with devices in the Apple ecosystem. And though Android-compatible portable trackers have also been around for a while, the ability to use distributed networking to make them work better is a recent development.

Google, as the primary author of Android and its ecosystem, developed the Find My Devices technology used by the Samsung Galaxy SmartTag 2 and Motorola Moto Tag, as well as numerous third-party devices. Now it has its own hardware, the Google Tag.

Trevor Noah and Google’s Isabelle Olsson talk about the new Google Tag at Made By Google 2026. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Even if the Google Tag doesn’t reach the same saturation as Apple’s tracking pucks, the little oblong locators with a prominent G stamped onto them are no doubt worth doing. AirTags have a 50% to 60% profit margin, according to some estimates, so as long as Google can manufacture them reasonably, they’ll join the worldwide Find Hub network, helping people locate all the stuff we lose every day.

I’m a ramblin’ man

I know people who dictate most everything – texts to friends, web searches, articles – and they’re remarkably smooth. I’ve never had that gift. When I try to dictate, I invariably devolve into sentence fragments, grunts and swear words.

Rambler, a new Gemini feature originally demoed at Google I/O 2026 in May, is a much more patient listener than most transcription apps or AIs. It understands those bits and pieces of conversation and threads them back into usable text.

I’m looking forward to seeing if I can stump it. I suppose I could also work on my speaking skills, too.

AI can translate ASL to text

Google demonstrated its sign-language-to-text (SL2T) language model, a way for people to communicate in American Sign Language by translating and transcribing their body motions.

Google’s Annie Jean-Baptiste uses sign-language-to-text to have a conversation with actor Daniel Durant. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

This is a very cool feature, but I’m more impressed with how it’s executed. The phone records a person using ASL, which sets off privacy bells and has me wondering what the company might do with that video.

But in fact, the “on-device model tracks the location of points on the signer, and only those geometric coordinates are sent to the server for translation,” according to Google. The video is immediately discarded while the sequence is translated into text.

HiLight starts at a surprising low point

HiLight looked like it would be an actual highlight of the Pixel 11 Pro line, but I have to admit I’m a little slack-jawed at what Google is shipping. I think the crowd at the event and even Noah were underwhelmed, too.

Replacing the temperature sensor on the Pixel 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL and 11 Pro Fold – I forgot that feature was there, sorry – HiLight is a circular LED near the cameras that can light up more than a typical smartphone flash. Reminiscent of Nothing’s inventive Glyph, the HiLight can light up in other colors and act as a notification alert when the phone is face down.

“Aaand… there it is.” The HiLight shows green when a contact calls. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

But all it can do right now is display an assigned color when one of your contacts calls you – purple for your partner or orange for your parents, for example – and light up in a swirl of colors when you activate the Gemini assistant. Surprisingly, the presenter said that it can’t do the color red.

Yeah, that’s it. Colors for phone calls, not texts, and an indicator that you’re using Gemini when you presumably just made a request of Gemini.

Trevor Noah looks incredulous that there isn’t more to the Pixel 11 Pro’s HiLight feature during Made By Google 2026. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Let’s hope Google just ran out of time and that there will be additional features that take advantage of the HiLight, and a way for developers to create their own interactions.

That little circle is just begging for a port of Doom. And to play The Odyssey the way Christopher Nolan intended.

Tech.title: Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro vs. Pixel 11 Pro XL: Google’s Latest Phones Compared
Tech.content:
Google unveiled a brand-new slate of handsets for 2026: the Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL and 11 Pro Fold. The Pixel 11 series has a number of improvements over its predecessors, including more efficient Tensor G6 processors, camera advancements such as Magic Capture and overall spec upgrades.

While there aren’t many design differences compared with the Pixel 10, the Pixel 11 Pro devices in particular do have one notable addition: HiLight. Initially rumored as the “Pixel Glow,” HiLight is essentially an array of ambient LED lights built around the camera’s flash that provide visual cues depending on the type of notification you’re getting. It hearkens back to the BlackBerry’s notification LED.

The Pixel 11 series also showcases many of Gemini Intelligence’s latest features, such as voice-to-text capabilities that filter out filler words when sending a message, or the ability to communicate in ASL via the Pixel camera.

The Pixel 11 series is now available to preorder. Wondering which new Pixel to buy? Here’s how the Pixel 11, 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL compare against one another.

Pixel 11 vs. 11 Pro/11 Pro XL: Design and display

The Pixel 11 Pro XL’s screen is brighter than previous Pixel Pro models.

At first glance, the Pixel 11 series doesn’t look too different from its predecessors. The Pixel 11 and 11 Pro still have a 6.3-inch OLED screen, and the 11 Pro XL has a 6.8-inch OLED display. The Pixel 11 has a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, but the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL both have peak brightness increased to 3,600 nits (up from 3,300 on the 10 Pro and 10 Pro XL).

One major design change is that the Pixel’s camera bar is now made of edge-to-edge glass, giving it a much more seamless look. This camera bar is also home to the new HiLight ambient LED feature, though it’s exclusive to just the Pixel 11 Pro devices.

The aim of the HiLight feature is to provide visual cues about who is calling you when the phone is face down. According to Google, the feature integrates with your contacts list, so your favorite contact’s custom color will light up if they’re trying to call you.

Size-wise, the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro both measure 6 by 2.8 by 0.3 inches and the Pixel 11 Pro XL is 6.4 by 3 by 0.3 inches. Interestingly, however, they seem to weigh a tiny bit less than the Pixel 10 series. The Pixel 11 weighs in at 6.9 ounces (down from 7.2 ounces), the 11 Pro is 7.2 ounces (down from 7.3 ounces), and the Pixel 11 Pro XL is 8 ounces (down from 8.2 ounces).

Let’s not forget the color options. The Pixel 11 is available in frost, pistachio, hibiscus and obsidian, while the 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL are available in canyon, olive, fog and obsidian (matte finish).

Pixel 11 vs. 11 Pro/11 Pro XL: Cameras

Software adds the biggest upgrades to the Pixel cameras.

For the most part, the Pixel 11 series has the same trio of rear cameras as its predecessors.

Pixel 11 series cameras compared

Wide-angle Ultrawide Telephoto Selfie Pixel 11 48 megapixels 13 megapixels 10.8 megapixels 10.5 megapixels Pixel 11 Pro/11 Pro XL 50 megapixels 48 megapixels 50 megapixels 42 megapixels

The big difference with the 11 series is that the 11 Pro cameras now have a Pro Zoom of up to 120x. The base Pixel 11 also has an upgraded 30x Super Zoom. Google also says that all three handsets have improved light sensitivity and larger sensors. The image sensors on the 11 Pro/11 Pro XL are larger than the ones on the Pixel 11’s cameras.

Many of the camera’s biggest improvements are software-based. For example, there’s a new Magic Capture mode that records a short video clip and then uses AI to select the best still frames from it. It definitely feels aimed at parents who want to take photos of their kids without worrying about getting the shot at the right time.

Another feature called Camera Looks lets you take photos with unique color and analog film styles. It’s similar to Photographic Styles on the iPhone.

Pixel 11 vs. 11 Pro/11 Pro XL: Storage, battery and other specs

One of the more notable shifts with the Pixel 11 series is that the 128GB model has been dropped from the lineup. Now, the lowest storage you can get is 256GB. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, but it does raise the price of entry.

Model Storage RAM US Price Pixel 11 256GB 12GB $899 Pixel 11 Pro 256GB 12GB $1,099 Pixel 11 Pro XL 256GB 12GB $1,199 Pixel 11 512GB 12GB $1,019 Pixel 11 Pro 512GB 16GB $1,219 Pixel 11 Pro XL 512GB 16GB $1,419 Pixel 11 Pro 1TB 16GB $1,499 Pixel 11 Pro XL 1TB 16GB $1,649

The Pixel 11 ships with a 4,985-mAh battery, the 11 Pro has 4,850 mAh and the 11 Pro has a 5,115 mAh. On paper, that might seem like a smaller capacity than their Pixel 10 counterparts, but Google says the Adaptive Battery feature on the Pixel 11 series should deliver over 30 hours of battery life. We’ll have to do some testing of our own to check those claims.

All the new Pixel 11 handsets are powered by the new Google Tensor G6, which should result in better power efficiency, faster browsing and faster app loading. Google also says that Gemini Nano should run with higher quality and lower latency on the Pixel 11 series thanks to the Tensor G6.
